flashcards.answer: Formation taxi procedures ensure safe, standardized ground movement of multiple aircraft. Lead directs coordination and communications, while Wing maintains safe spacing and monitors Lead while completing checklist items.
A section takeoff is when both aircraft maintain formation integrity and position through the entire takeoff roll. It develops confidence and skill in holding formation during critical flight phases.
A maneuver used to trade formation positions. Lead directs the change with a signal or radio call, and Wing assumes Lead responsibilities while the former Lead transitions to Wing.

A looser variation of parade formation allowing Wing more flexibility for checks, clearing, or relaxation. Commonly used during in-flight checks or frequency changes, cruise formation reduces Wing fatigue while maintaining formation integrity.

The crossunder repositions the Wing aircraft to the opposite side of Lead for clearing, sun angle, pattern entry, or maneuver setup. It requires precise, smooth control due to close proximity to Lead.

An interval takeoff uses timing separation between aircraft brake releases to create safe spacing for takeoff when a section takeoff is hazardous. Aircraft depart individually, then rendezvous in parade formation.

Parade formation is the foundation of formation flying. It emphasizes precise positioning, smooth control, and disciplined monitoring of Lead. Most formation training focuses on mastering Wing parade formation.

N - Use this procedure for any of the following: red OIL PX annunciator illuminated, amber OIL PX annunciator illuminated, oil pressure fluctuations, oil temperature out of limits, or visibly confirmed leaking oil from the aircraft.

N - Due to the sensitivity of the signal conditioning unit, a single, momentary illumination of the amber OIL PX caution while maneuvering

flashcards.companionGroupID: emergency engine shutdown on the ground
flashcards.prompt: EMERGENCY ENGINE SHUTDOWN ON THE GROUND

flashcards.answer:
(2W/2C/5N)
C - Illumination of the OBOGS TEMP message indicates a failure of the OBOGS heat exchanger, and is considered a failure of the
OBOGS system.
W - Emergency oxygen bottle provides approximately 10 minutes of oxygen. If aircraft pressure altitude is above 10,000 feet MSL, ensure the aircraft reaches an altitude of 10,000 feet MSL or lower prior to exhaustion of the emergency oxygen supply or the effects of hypoxia may incapacitate the crew.
W - The OBOGS concentrator may malfunction resulting in zeolite dust in the breathing system without an illumination of the OBOGS FAIL light. Indications of this malfunction include respiratory irritation, coughing, or the presence of white dust in the oxygen mask. Inhalation of zeolite dust should be avoided.
C - When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe at a rate and depth slightly less than normal to preclude hyperventilation.
N - If physiological symptoms are recognized, immediate access to a pure and secure source of oxygen is the best course of action to expedite recovery. If the cockpit altitude is above 10,000 feet, pulling the GREEN RING is required since ambient cockpit air contains insufficient oxygen pressure to support physiological requirements. At a cockpit altitude of 10,000 feet or below, pulling the GREEN RING is optional as ambient cockpit air contains sufficient oxygen pressure to support
physiological requirements.
N - When the emergency oxygen system is actuated, high pressure air may make verbal communication with the other crewmember or
ATC more difficult.
N - Once activated, ejection seat emergency oxygen cannot be shut off and will provide oxygen flow until the cylinder is depleted (10 minutes). Since the emergency oxygen system is not regulated, it is normal for pressure to gradually decrease to the point it feels like the oxygen is depleted before reaching 10
minutes of use, however oxygen is still being
supplied.
N - Sharply pull the green ring up and aft to activate the emergency oxygen system. Several up and aft pull attempts may be required to
fully activate oxygen flow.
N - Pull force to activate the emergency oxygen
system may be as high as 40 pounds.

(1C/1N)
N - If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the engine-driven high pressure fuel pump is suction feeding. Engine operation with high pressure pump suction feeding is limited to 10 hours.
C - Unless a greater emergency exists, do not reset BOOST PUMP circuit breaker (left front console) if open.

(3W/1N)
W - To avoid injury, grasp handle and pull sharply toward abdomen, keeping elbows against the body.
W - The emergency escape system incorporates an explosive canopy fracturing system. The force of detonation blows numerous shards and small fragments outward from the canopy and into the cockpit. Some metallic fragments may be extremely hot and may cause burns upon contact with the skin. Aircrew should ensure exposed skin is covered, the oxygen mask is on, and visor is down prior to ejection or actuating the CFS system to prevent injury from shards and hot fragments.
W - When ejecting over mountainous terrain exceeding 8000 feet MSL, the manual override (MOR) handle should be used to manually separate from the seat and deploy the parachute.
N - If ejecting at low speed, one or both sets of risers may remain velcroed together following seat separation. This may create a slight increase in descent rate and/or an uncommanded turn. Manually separate the risers if time permits. The steering lines (toggles) are located on the backside of each of the front risers. To counter any uncommanded turns, unstow the opposite steering line or use risers
for controllability.

(1W)
W - After a stop which required maximum effort braking and if overheated brakes are suspected, do not taxi into or park in a congested area until brakes have had sufficient time to cool. Do not set parking brake.

(1W/1N)
W - Under varying conditions of fire and/or smoke where aircraft control is jeopardized, the pilot has the option of actuating CFS or
ejecting.
N - If a faulty component can be identified as the source of smoke and fumes, turn defective unit off or pull respective circuit breaker. Circuit breakers for items on the hot battery bus are not accessible in flight.
flashcards.companionGroupID: smoke and fume elimination electrical fire

flashcards.answer:
(1C)
C - Higher power settings may aggravate the
existing condition.

(4W)
W - Illumination of the fire warning light accompanied by one or more of the following indications is confirmation of an engine fire: smoke; flames; engine vibration; unusual sounds; high ITT; and fluctuating oil pressure,
oil temperature, or hydraulic pressure.
W - A fire warning light with no accompanying indication is not a confirmed fire. Do not shut down an engine for an unconfirmed fire.
W - High engine compartment temperatures resulting from a bleed air leak may cause illumination of the fire warning light. Reducing the PCL setting towards IDLE will decrease the amount of bleed air and possibly extinguish the fire warning light; however, advancing the PCL might be required to intercept the ELP. Regardless of reducing or advancing the PCL, continue to investigate
for indications confirming an engine fire.
W - If the fire cannot be confirmed, the fire warning system may be at fault and should be tested as conditions permit. If only one fire loop annunciator is illuminated (top or bottom half only), a false fire indication may
exist if the other loop tests good.

(3W/5N)
N - Zoom results with an engine still producing a usable torque (>6%) will be several hundred to several thousand feet higher in altitude
gained.
N - Each low altitude zoom capability chart depicted in Figure 3-2, Figure 3-3, and Figure 3-4 represents a no engine condition. Each chart assumes the pilot will not perform any action prior to actual engine failure.
N - If experiencing uncommanded power changes/loss of power/uncommanded propeller feather or compressor stalls, refer to
appropriate procedure.
N - Propeller will not feather unless the PCL is
fully in OFF.
W - If a suitable landing surface is available, turn immediately to intercept the nearest suitable point on the ELP. Any delay could result in insufficient gliding distance to reach a landing surface.
W - Do not delay decision to eject below 2000
feet AGL.
W - Airstart procedure is not recommended below 2000 feet AGL, as primary attention should be to eject or safely recover the aircraft.
N - Crosscheck N1 against other engine indications to assess condition of engine and determine if an airstart is warranted. At 125 KIAS, an engine which has flamed out will rotate below 8% N1 and indicate 0% N1. The engine oil pressure indicator may display oil pressures up to 4 psi with or without the engine seized.

(2W/2N)
W - If insufficient runway remains to land
straight ahead, consider immediate ejection.
W - Do not sacrifice aircraft control while troubleshooting or lowering gear with emergency system.
N - The pilot should select IDLE to use the increased drag of the not yet feathered propeller or select OFF to reduce the sink rate.
N - With a loss of hydraulic pressure, landing gear and flaps cannot be lowered by normal means.
flashcards.companionGroupID: engine failure immediately after takeoff sufficient runway remaining straight ahead
flashcards.prompt: ENGINE FAILURE IMMEDIATELY AFTER TAKEOFF (SUFFICIENT RUNWAY REMAINING STRAIGHT AHEAD)

flashcards.answer:
(5W/2C/4N)
W - Aircraft may float while approaching touchdown with the propeller feathered more than observed while conducting practice forced landing at 4-6% torque. Energy management is critical to achieving targeted touchdown position. Landing ground roll distance will increase with the propeller feathered.
W - Landing on an unprepared surface may cause structural damage making it impossible to open the canopy or fracture it using the CFS.
W - Engine failure or shutdown will completely disable the bleed air system. Depending on environmental conditions, this may cause significant canopy icing and/or fogging, and severely hamper visibility, especially from
the rear cockpit.
C - Ejection is recommended if a suitable landing area is not available. If circumstances dictate an emergency landing and ejection is not possible or the ejection system malfunctions, the pilot may perform an ELP to an unprepared
surface or ditch the aircraft. The aircraft structure can survive either type of forced landing; however, the risk of injury increases significantly due to crash loads and the complexity of ground or water egress.
C - Inducing yaw (side slipping) with a known engine/oil malfunction could result in impaired windshield visibility due to oil leakage
spraying onto the windshield.
W - If landing on an unprepared surface or ditching, do not extend the landing gear. Flaps will not be available without emergency gear
extension.
N - Normal safe indications with electrical power, when the emergency extension system has been used to lower the gear, are two green main gear lights, two red main door lights, green nose gear light, and red light in
handle.
W - Do not lower flaps LDG until landing is assured. Drag will increase dramatically once landing flaps are lowered.
N - Selecting either TO or LDG flaps will extend the flaps to the commanded position if the landing gear has been extended using the emergency extension system and if battery power is available.
N - Landing gear/flap retraction is not possible when the emergency extension system has been used.
N - Nose wheel steering is unavailable with an inoperative engine. Maintain directional control with rudder and differential braking.

(2W/3C/7N)
N - Mid range is a physical PCL angle that approximates the midway position between IDLE and MAX.
N - A PCL position above IDLE will provide the
best chance for the engine to recover.
N - A mid-range PCL position will minimize the potential of engine overtorque and/or overtemperature when the PMU is turned OFF.
C - There is a potential for ITT limits to be exceeded if the PMU switch is turned OFF with ITT ≥820 °C.
C - Ground idle will not be available during landing rollout and taxi. Plan for increased landing distances due to higher IDLE N1
(approximately 67%).
N - With constant airspeed and torque, RPM can be considered stable if below 40% and no upward change for a 3-second period.
N - If NP indicator is displaying red X’s, switching the PMU to NORM and back OFF will reset the PMU and should restore the NP indication.
N - Propeller should come out of feather within
15-20 seconds.
W - If rate of descent (indicated on the VSI while stabilized at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and 4-6% torque) is greater than 1500 ft/min, increase torque as necessary (up to 131%) to achieve approximately
1350-1500 ft/min rate of descent. If engine power is insufficient to produce a rate of descent less than 1500 ft/min, set PCL to
OFF.
N - The pilot should consider moving the PCL through the full range of motion to determine power available.
C - Consideration should be given to leaving the
engine operating with PCL at mid range.
W - With the PROP SYS circuit breaker pulled and the PMU switch OFF, the feather dump solenoid will not be powered. The propeller will feather at a slower rate as oil pressure decreases and the feathering spring takes effect. Glide performance will be considerably reduced and it may not be possible to
intercept or fly the emergency landing pattern.
flashcards.companionGroupID: uncommanded power changes loss of power uncommanded propeller feather
flashcards.prompt:
UNCOMMANDED POWER CHANGES/LOSS OF
POWER/UNCOMMANDED PROPELLER FEATHER

flashcards.answer:
(1W/1N)
N - Setting the DEFOG switch to ON automatically selects high bleed air inflow and will alleviate back pressure on the engine compressor.
W - When the engine is so underpowered that high rates of descent occur, any delay in shutting down the engine to feather the propeller may result in insufficient altitude to reach a suitable landing site.

(2W/1C/1N)
W - Improperly positioning the control stick/elevator aft of the neutral position may significantly delay or prevent the aircraft from recovering from an OCF/spin which could result in loss of aircraft and/or crew.
N - Cycling of control positions or applying antispin controls prematurely can aggravate aircraft motion and significantly delay recovery.
W -
Recommended minimum altitude for ejection
is 6000 feet AGL.
C - Power-on and inverted departures or spins will result in high loads on the engine and torque shaft. If an inverted or power-on departure is encountered, land as soon as conditions permit. The pilot should suspect possible engine damage and may experience unusual engine operation accompanied by
low oil pressure or CHIP detector warning. In all cases of inverted or power-on departures, the engine shall be inspected by qualified
maintenance personnel after flight.

(4W/3C)
W - Airstart attempts outside of the airstart envelope may be unsuccessful or result in engine overtemperature. Consideration should be given to ensure airstarts are attempted within the airstart envelope (125-200 KIAS for sea level to 15,000 feet, or 135-200 KIAS for 15,001 to 20,000 feet).
W - Do not delay ejection while attempting airstart
at low altitude if below 2000 feet AGL.
W - PCL must be in OFF to feather the propeller, and ensure proper starter, ignition, boost pump, and PMU operation during airstart.
C - Ensure PCL is in OFF; otherwise, fuel may
be prematurely introduced during start.
C - Continuous operation with the BOOST PUMP switch in the ON position will cause damage to the engine-driven low pressure fuel pump. Upon landing, notify maintenance of the duration of flight with BOOST PUMP
switch in the ON position.
C - If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, discontinue the airstart attempt and proceed to IF AIRSTART IS UNSUCCESSFUL due to
suspected mechanical failure.
W - Movement of the PCL above IDLE before N1 stabilizes at approximately 67% will cause an increase in fuel flow which may cause engine
failure due to a severe ITT overtemperature.
C - If there is no rise in ITT within 10 seconds after fuel flow indications, place the PCL to OFF and abort the start.

(5W/2N)
N - In a situation requiring immediate ground egress, the ejection system has the capability for 0/0 ejection.
W - Failure to ensure that the ISS mode selector is set to SOLO may result in the inadvertent ejection of one or both seats.
W - Failure to insert both ejection seat safety pins (if occupied) before ground egress may result in inadvertent activation of ejection sequence and subsequent injury or death when performing
emergency ground egress.
W - If the canopy fracturing system malfunctions in conjunction with a canopy latch failure in the locked position, ejection may be the only option remaining to exit the aircraft. Aircrew shall remove the ejection seat safety pin and ensure shoulder straps, lap straps, and leg restraint garters are still attached prior to pulling
ejection handle.
W - To prevent injury, ensure oxygen mask is on and visor is down prior to actuating the CFS system.
W - Each internal CFS handle activates only the CFS charge for the respective transparency. Both internal CFS handles must be activated in order to fracture both transparencies (if required).
N - Oxygen hose, emergency oxygen hose, communication leads, and anti-G suit hose will pull free while vacating cockpit and leg restraint lines will pull through leg restraint garter D rings if released with quick-release
lever.

(1W)
W - Higher power settings accompanied by high ITT may aggravate the existing condition. However, if ITT is within limits reducing power could result in engine flameout.

(2N)
N - note and report to MX the degree and duration of any overtemperature
N - If start is initiated with PCL in the OFF position, abort by reselecting AUTO/RESET on the STARTER switch. If start is initiated with PCL out of the OFF position, but not past the IDLE gate, abort by placing the PCL to OFF
or reselecting AUTO/RESET on the
STARTER switch. If the PCL is past the
IDLE gate, abort by placing the PCL to OFF.

(4W/2C)
W - If the engine should fail while flying the PEL, refer to the Engine Failure During Flight checklist, and transition to the Forced Landing
procedure.
W - If rate of descent (indicated on the VSI while stabilized at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and 4 to 6% torque) is greater than 1500 ft/min, increase torque as necessary (up to 131%) to achieve approximately 1350 to 1500 ft/min rate of descent. If engine power is insufficient to produce a rate of descent less than 1500 ft/min, set PCL to OFF.
W - Once on profile, if engine is vibrating excessively, or if indications of failure are imminent, set PCL to OFF.
W - Engine failure or shutdown will completely disable the bleed air system. Depending on environmental conditions, this may cause significant canopy icing and/or fogging, severely hampering visibility, especially
from the rear cockpit.
C - Inducing yaw (side slipping) with a known engine/oil malfunction could result in impaired windshield visibility due to oil leakage
spraying onto the windshield.
C - At higher temperature and pressure altitudes, power response will be delayed. Airspeeds below 110 KIAS on ELP final, in combination with transitioning to a high flare, may lead to a hard landing resulting in landing
gear component failure.

events.overview: This event is your introduction to operating in the T-6B cockpit. You will practice checklist discipline, challenge-action-response procedures, crew coordination, ground handling signals, and safety checks before entering and leaving the aircraft. You will also begin building cockpit familiarity through blind cockpit checks and repeated strap-in practice.

events.overview: This event builds on basic cockpit procedures by introducing abnormal starts and ground emergencies. You will practice identifying no starts, hung starts, hot starts, fire indications, emergency shutdown procedures, and emergency ground egress while continuing to build checklist discipline and CRM.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The PMU will often automatically terminate a bad start, but you still need to recognize the indications and be ready to manually abort.

children.text: No Start: No ITT rise within 10 seconds after fuel flow indications.
Hung Start: N1 stops increasing normally.
Hot Start: ITT is rising rapidly and appears likely to exceed 1000°C.
ITT appears likely to stay between 871°C and 1000°C for more than 5 seconds.
The red BATT BUS warning appears during start.
The ST READY advisory extinguishes during the start sequence.
The PCL is moved incorrectly during start.

items.text: You should also manually abort if:
Any overtemperature should be noted and reported to maintenance.

children.text: PCL to OFF.
Or reselect STARTER switch to AUTO/RESET if appropriate.

items.text: If a start must be aborted:
After any aborted start where fuel was introduced, perform a motoring run.

children.text: PCL OFF.
Ignition switch NORM.
Prop area clear.
Starter switch MANUAL for 20 seconds.
Starter switch NORM.

items.text: The goal of the motoring run is to clear residual fuel and lower ITT.
Ensure the ST READY advisory remains on for at least 3 seconds before selecting AUTO/RESET.
If the ST READY advisory extinguishes at any point during the start sequence, the PMU no longer provides automatic start protection.
Once ST READY is lost, the start must be manually aborted.
If the PCL is still before idle, abort by moving the PCL to OFF or selecting AUTO/RESET.
If the PCL is already past the idle gate, abort with PCL OFF.

sections.title: Loss of START READY During Start

items.text: The red BATT BUS warning during start is a serious indication.
It may appear before the displays fail.
If it appears, MFD failure and the inability to monitor the start may be imminent.
The primary indication of an engine fire is illumination of the FIRE annunciators.

children.text: Visible smoke or flames.
High or fluctuating fuel flow.
High ITT.
Notification from tower, ground crew, or another aircraft.

items.text: If a fire is suspected, execute Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground and Emergency Ground Egress if required.
N/W/C focus: Review the associated WARNINGs, CAUTIONs, and NOTEs before the event so you know when a suspected ground fire becomes a confirmed emergency.

children.text: Engine fire.
Prop strike.
Chip light.
Aircraft departing the prepared surface.
Any other major ground emergency.
PCL OFF.
Firewall Shutoff Handle PULL.
Emergency Ground Egress as required.

items.text: N/W/C focus: Do not let checklist execution outrun aircraft control or crew coordination during a high-stress ground emergency.

sections.title: Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground

items.text: The aircraft has 0/0 ejection capability, but ground egress should be completed once the aircraft is stopped and the engine is shut down.

children.text: ISS to SOLO.
Seat safety pin installed.
Parking brake as required.
Canopy open.
Remove CFS safety pins.
Rotate and pull CFS handles.
Release restraints and garters.
BAT, GEN, and AUX BAT switches OFF.
Evacuate aircraft.

items.text: If the canopy cannot be opened:
Oxygen mask on and visor down before activating the CFS.
Both cockpits must activate their own CFS handles if both transparencies need to fracture.
N/W/C focus: Oxygen mask on and visor down before actuating CFS, and remember both cockpits must actuate their own CFS handles if both transparencies must fracture.
The Canopy Fracturing System clears a path through the canopy during ejection.
Front cockpit uses a stronger explosive charge because the front windscreen is thicker.
Rear cockpit uses a lighter charge because the rear transparency is thinner.
Minimum uncontrolled ejection altitude is 6000 feet AGL.
Minimum controlled ejection altitude is 2000 feet AGL.
Controlled ejections rely heavily on CRM to split checklist tasks and maximize survivability.
The ejection seat is a Martin-Baker system capable of 0/0 ejection.
N/W/C focus: Treat seat pins, ISS position, and canopy-fracturing actions as no-fail items because mistakes here can injure the crew on the ground.
loss of start ready light during start sequence
emergency engine shutdown on the ground

events.overview: This event introduces emergency situations that can happen during takeoff and flight. You will learn how to respond to aborts, engine failures, aircraft departures from the runway, forced landings, and airstarts while focusing on aircraft control, decision making, and when to stop troubleshooting and commit to landing or ejecting.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: If it becomes necessary to abort, aircraft control is the priority.
Focus on maintaining directional control while stopping on the remaining runway.

children.text: PCL to IDLE.
Brakes as required.

items.text: Heavy braking can overheat the brakes.
If maximum braking was used, do not taxi into a congested area or set the parking brake until the brakes cool.
N/W/C focus: Hot brakes after maximum-effort stopping can create a second emergency, so do not set the parking brake or taxi into a congested area until they cool.
If it appears likely the aircraft will depart the runway or taxiway, execute Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground.
The priority is to stop the aircraft and shut the engine down before further damage occurs.

children.text: Total loss of power.
Rapid reduction in airspeed.

items.text: Early ejection may be the safest option if there is not enough runway remaining.

children.text: Maintain at least 110 knots.
PCL as required.
Pull Emergency Landing Gear Handle if required.
Flaps as required.

items.text: If hydraulic pressure is lost, gear and flaps cannot be lowered normally.
Below 2000 feet AGL, avoid wasting time troubleshooting.
If there is not enough runway to land straight ahead, immediate ejection may be the best option.
N/W/C focus: Below 2000 feet AGL, do not burn altitude troubleshooting when the safer answer is straight-ahead landing or early ejection.

children.text: Airstart.
Forced landing.
Ejection.

items.text: An engine failure in flight creates three possible paths:

children.text: Loss of power and airspeed.
Rapid drop in N1, torque, and ITT.
Propeller moving toward feather.
GEN, FUEL PX, OIL PX, and OBOGS warnings.
Establish at least 125 knots.
PCL to OFF.
Intercept the nearest suitable ELP.
Attempt an airstart if warranted.

items.text: Pulling the PCL fully to OFF feathers the propeller and improves glide performance.

children.text: Firewall Shutoff Handle PULL.
Execute forced landing or eject.

items.text: If an airstart is not appropriate or unsuccessful:
Do not delay the ejection decision below 2000 feet AGL.
N/W/C focus: Pulling the PCL fully to OFF is what feathers the prop and improves glide; partial movement does not buy the same margin.
The Immediate Airstart is used at low altitude when thrust is urgently needed.
It is faster than the full PMU NORM procedure.

children.text: PCL OFF.
Starter switch AUTO/RESET.
PCL to IDLE above 13% N1.
Monitor ITT, N1, and oil pressure.

items.text: If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, discontinue the attempt.
If there is no ITT rise within 10 seconds after fuel flow, abort the start.
Useful power is not available until approximately 67% N1.

children.text: PCL OFF.
Firewall Shutoff Handle PULL.
Forced landing or eject.

items.text: PMU NORM is the preferred and simplest airstart method.
Use it if the PMU FAIL warning is not illuminated.

children.text: 125 to 200 knots from sea level to 15,000 feet.
135 to 200 knots from 15,001 to 20,000 feet.
PCL OFF.
Firewall Shutoff Handle down.
Bleed Air Inflow OFF.
Boost Pump ON.
Ignition ON.
Starter switch AUTO/RESET.

items.text: Move the PCL to IDLE above 13% N1.
Do not move the PCL above IDLE before N1 stabilizes around 67%.
Each airstart attempt can cost more than 1200 feet of altitude.

children.text: PCL as required.
Starter switch NORM.
Verify GEN ON.
Bleed Air Inflow NORM.
Execute a PEL.

items.text: PMU OFF airstarts are used if the PMU FAIL warning is illuminated.
This method increases workload because the pilot manually controls fuel introduction.
The same airstart envelope and altitude considerations apply.
PMU OFF starts are more sensitive to PCL movement and can more easily lead to an overtemperature.
Use this procedure only when PMU NORM is unavailable.
Establish a safe airspeed and glide profile before troubleshooting.
If a suitable runway or landing surface is available, immediately turn toward it.
Every second spent troubleshooting reduces glide distance.
Below 2000 feet AGL, focus on landing or ejecting rather than trying to save the engine.
Airstarts should only be attempted when altitude, airspeed, and position allow.
The remaining FAM2201 EPs all reward the same habit pattern: maintain flying airspeed, turn toward a landing option early, and do not waste altitude troubleshooting below decision altitude.
Uncommanded power changes, loss of power, or an uncommanded prop feather should be treated as a deteriorating engine situation until proven otherwise.
Smoke and fume elimination is about keeping the cockpit breathable and visible long enough to land as soon as practical.
A fire warning in flight is only a confirmed fire when it is backed up by other indications. If confirmed, secure the engine and commit to forced landing or ejection as required.
Controlled ejection is a life-saving decision, not a last-second failure. Make it early enough that altitude, airspeed, and aircraft attitude still favor survival.
N/W/C focus: The warnings, cautions, and notes on these EPs mainly reinforce one habit pattern: identify the branch early and commit before altitude and options disappear.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the priorities simple: aviate first, point the aircraft toward the best landing option early, and do not burn altitude troubleshooting below decision altitude.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: A CHIP warning indicates possible metal contamination in the engine oil system.
Severe contamination can lead to engine failure with little warning.

children.text: PCL to minimum power required to intercept the ELP.
Avoid unnecessary PCL movements.
Execute a PEL.

items.text: Higher power settings can make the problem worse.
N/W/C focus: Treat higher power settings and unnecessary PCL movement as risk multipliers once a CHIP indication makes engine health questionable.

children.text: Red OIL PX warning.
Amber OIL PX caution.
Oil pressure fluctuations.
Oil temperature outside normal limits.
Visible oil leaking from the aircraft.

items.text: A momentary amber OIL PX during maneuvering may not indicate a malfunction.
If both red and amber OIL PX messages appear with normal oil pressure, it may indicate an SCU failure.

children.text: Terminate maneuvering.
Check oil pressure.
Continue only if oil pressure is normal.

items.text: If only the amber OIL PX caution appears:

children.text: PCL to minimum power needed to intercept the ELP.
Avoid unnecessary power changes.
Execute a PEL.

items.text: If the red OIL PX warning appears, amber OIL PX remains illuminated for more than 5 seconds, oil pressure fluctuates, or oil temperature is out of limits:
N/W/C focus: A momentary caution during maneuvering is not the same as a persistent warning tied to bad oil indications; know the difference before you overreact or underreact.

sections.title: Oil System Malfunction / Low Oil Pressure

children.text: Blocked fuel line.
Fuel leak.
Low pressure pump failure.
Oil scavenge pump failure.
Fuel pressure switch failure.

items.text: Low fuel pressure may be caused by:

children.text: FUEL PX warning.
Fuel feed pressure below 10 PSI.

Execute a PEL.
BOOST PUMP switch ON.

items.text: Do not reset the BOOST PUMP circuit breaker unless a greater emergency exists.
If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the high pressure fuel pump is suction feeding and engine operation is time limited.
N/W/C focus: If suction-feed indications persist, the engine is operating on borrowed time and the landing plan needs to get more aggressive, not less.
High fuel flow is considered 800 PPH or greater.

children.text: Execute a PEL.

items.text: High power settings combined with high ITT can make the condition worse.
Reducing power too aggressively can also risk engine flameout.

children.text: HYD FL LO caution.
Hydraulic pressure below 1800 PSI.
Rapidly decreasing hydraulic pressure.
EHYD PX LO caution.
Landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering should be considered unavailable.

items.text: If normal hydraulic pressure is lost:

children.text: Emergency landing gear and flap extension system should be considered unavailable.

items.text: Gear and flaps should generally be lowered early if hydraulic fluid loss is suspected.
If all hydraulic fluid is lost, a gear-up landing may become necessary.
Low hydraulic pressure may require emergency landing gear extension.
Use this procedure only when directed by another malfunction checklist.
Pulling the Emergency Landing Gear Handle extends the gear regardless of gear handle position.

children.text: Landing gear and flaps cannot be retracted.
Green gear lights.
Red gear door lights.
Red light in the gear handle.

items.text: Normal indications after emergency extension are:
The pull may require significant force, sometimes over 80 pounds.
After landing, do not taxi if any gear position light indicates unsafe.
N/W/C focus: Once emergency extension is used, gear and flaps are not coming back up, so do not pull the handle unless another malfunction actually calls for it.
OBOGS FAIL indicates a malfunction in the oxygen system.

children.text: Heat exchanger failure.
Bleed air supply problems.
Electrical failures.
Excessive leakage.
Reduced oxygen flow.
Breathing difficulty.
Hypoxia symptoms.
Pull the Green Ring as required.
Descend below 10,000 feet MSL.
OBOGS Supply Lever OFF.
Check emergency oxygen hose.
Normalize breathing.

items.text: The emergency oxygen bottle lasts approximately 10 minutes.

children.text: Pressurization switch to RAM/DUMP.
Bleed Air Inflow OFF.
Oxygen mask may be removed if required.

items.text: N/W/C focus: Oxygen and cockpit-pressure problems can turn into a crew-survivability issue quickly, so know when descent and checklist execution take priority over everything else.
A runaway trim condition occurs when trim moves without pilot input.
The trim interrupt button or trim disconnect switch can be used to stop unwanted trim movement.
Pulling a trim circuit breaker makes that trim system inoperative.
Loss of rudder trim may significantly increase workload.
Maintain aircraft control first, then isolate the malfunction.
A PEL is used anytime a malfunction exists that may worsen before landing.
The goal is to safely reach the nearest suitable runway before the condition becomes an emergency.
Most system malfunctions in this event eventually lead to a PEL.

children.text: Maintaining aircraft control.
Intercepting the ELP early.
Avoiding unnecessary power changes.
Preserving the aircraft systems that remain.

items.text: N/W/C focus: The big warning here is not to let a marginal profile turn into a low-altitude salvage attempt. Use available power early and stay honest about runway makeability.
Intercept the nearest suitable ELP early.
Avoid unnecessary power changes when a system malfunction is already developing.
Land as soon as practical before a manageable malfunction becomes a major emergency.
Many of these procedures are less about fixing the issue and more about preserving enough aircraft to safely land.
oil system malfunction or low oil pressure

studyNotes.summary: Most of these malfunctions are handled by preserving what still works, minimizing extra power or configuration changes, and getting to the nearest suitable runway early.

You will practice spotting warning signs, deciding when a PEL is warranted, flying the emergency landing pattern early, and using DEGA and PEL(P) concepts to preserve enough energy and runway options before the situation becomes a forced landing or ejection scenario.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Engine failure may arrive with little warning, but several signs point to a degrading engine before total power loss.

children.text: Excessive vibration, smoke, fumes, or unusual engine noise.
CHIP annunciation, oil-pressure problems, low fuel pressure, or high fuel flow.
Uncommanded power changes, loss of power, uncommanded propeller feather, or compressor stalls.

items.text: If any condition makes engine reliability doubtful, plan for a PEL immediately instead of waiting for a confirmed failure.
N/W/C focus: The warning here is indecision. Once engine reliability is doubtful, delaying the turn to a runway is usually the bigger mistake than acting early.
A PEL is used when engine failure is suspected or directed by checklist, but usable power still exists.

children.text: Turn toward the nearest suitable field.
Climb or accelerate to DEGA.
Keep the aircraft clean until configuration changes are actually needed.
Use available power early to stay on profile.

items.text: Do not delay configuration changes to try to rescue a low-energy profile late. If power is available in a PEL, use it.
N/W/C focus: In a PEL, power is still a tool. Use it early to stay on profile instead of waiting until the runway picture is already unrecoverable.
PEL(P) simulates the same problem from inside the landing pattern and trains you to intercept the ELP by or before Low Key.

children.text: Turn, clean, check, and plan.
Use boost pump and ignition only when an airstart would be appropriate.
Reduce power on the ELP, lower gear when appropriate, and complete the pattern with minimum 120 KIAS discipline.

items.text: High Key, Low Key, and DEGA calculations matter because they tell you whether a paved field remains reachable and whether you still have recovery options.
N/W/C focus: Preserve glide distance until landing is assured; do not trade away runway makeability with early drag or late, desperate corrections.
This event rewards early judgment more than troubleshooting depth.
If the engine worsens during the PEL, transition immediately to Engine Failure During Flight and then Forced Landing or Eject as required.
Do not lower landing flaps until landing is assured. Preserve glide distance until the runway is actually made.

studyNotes.summary: The event is about acting early. If engine reliability is in doubt, get the airplane pointed at a runway and fly the PEL profile before the problem takes that option away.

items.text: At low altitude, converting excess airspeed into altitude buys time for an airstart, landing setup, or ejection decision.
N/W/C focus: Engine indications matter because they drive the branch. A flameout, seizure, or prop issue does not buy the same restart or glide options.
The initial engine-failure flow is zoom or glide, PCL OFF, intercept the ELP, and attempt an airstart only if warranted.
Immediate Airstart is used when thrust is urgently needed and time does not permit the full restart setup.

children.text: PCL must be OFF first so the prop feathers and the restart is configured correctly.
If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, stop the attempt.
If ITT does not rise within 10 seconds after fuel flow, abort the start.
Do not advance the PCL above IDLE before N1 stabilizes around 67 percent.

items.text: Airstarts below 2000 feet AGL are usually a trap. Below that altitude, primary attention belongs on landing or ejecting.
N/W/C focus: Airstarts below 2000 feet AGL are usually a trap. Below that, landing or ejecting should dominate your thinking.

sections.title: Engine Failure During Flight and Airstarts

items.text: Forced landing is used when the engine is inoperative or power is insufficient for continued flight.
The forced landing profile differs from a PEL because low energy is corrected by delaying drag, not by using power that no longer exists.

items.text: N/W/C focus: Do not spend the last useful bit of glide margin trying to rescue a bad picture with configuration changes that come too early or too late.
Ejection is a life-saving action, not a failure, and it must be chosen before altitude and airspeed margins are gone.
The three ejection categories are immediate, time-critical, and controlled ejection.

children.text: Controlled ejection recommended above 2000 feet AGL.

items.text: The number one ejection failure is failure to pull the handle. Make the decision early.
N/W/C focus: The seat can save you only if you decide in time. Do not postpone the pull waiting for a cleaner aircraft attitude or a prettier altitude number.

studyNotes.summary: The decision chain is simple but unforgiving: recognize the failure, preserve energy, choose between restart, landing, or ejection, and do not waste the altitude you need for the next step.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Crosswind work here is less about learning a new technique and more about setting the picture early enough that you never end up chasing lineup late.

children.text: Before takeoff, note wind direction from tower and the windsock so you already know which controls will be in as the roll starts.
Start with aileron into the wind, reduce that input as speed builds, and use rudder to stop weathervaning and keep the nose aligned with the runway.
Rotate firmly at takeoff speed so the aircraft does not skip sideways off the upwind wheel, then level the wings and crab into the wind after liftoff.
Carry a crab on downwind as needed to hold the proper track, then use a wing-low final so drift is gone before touchdown.
In the approach turn, adjust bank and power early enough to avoid overshooting or undershooting final.
On final and through the flare, keep the upwind wing down, align the nose with rudder, and increase aileron as the airplane slows.

For full stops, touchdown should be on the upwind main first and crosswind controls stay in through rollout. For touch-and-goes, hold the crosswind picture through the ground roll and rotate at 90 KIAS.
Wave off if more than 45 degrees of bank is required or if side motion, drift, or crab remain unresolved.
In gusty conditions, add one-half the gust factor to final approach speed, but no more than 10 knots.
Brakes are for directional help only after the aircraft is below 80 KIAS and fully settled on the runway.
Common traps are too little aileron at the start of the roll, failing to reduce aileron as speed builds, holding a crab into touchdown, and trying to salvage a bad picture instead of waving off.

items.text: An abort is for any abnormal or unsafe condition before max abort speed, but the priority never changes: keep the airplane under control first, then stop it on the remaining runway.

children.text: Abort cues include blown tires, smoke or fuel leak, fire or chip indications, rising ITT, fluctuating oil pressure, bird strike, obstacles, or any malfunction that makes the takeoff unsafe to continue.
Immediate actions are PCL to IDLE and brakes as required while maintaining directional control with rudder and nosewheel steering.
Call the abort over ICS per local SOP, but do not let radio work get ahead of keeping the airplane straight.
Maximum braking is one smooth, increasing application as the aircraft slows. Do not pump or slam the brakes.
Above 80 KIAS, braking is less effective because lift is still unloading the wheels, so be cautious about aggressive pedal input and watch for directional-control problems.
If directional control is being lost, release braking immediately and reapply cautiously once the airplane is straight again.
If you have to cross a lowered BAK-15 during the stop, release the brakes before passing it and resume braking once clear.

items.text: N/W/C focus: There is no anti-skid, so do not brake before full weight is on wheels. After maximum-effort braking, do not set the parking brake or taxi into a congested area until the brakes cool, and do not request the barrier.
If the aircraft is about to depart, or has already departed, the prepared surface, stop trying to save the rollout and transition immediately to shutdown and egress decisions.

children.text: Execute Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground with PCL OFF and FIREWALL SHUTOFF HANDLE PULL.
Emergency Ground Egress is then as required based on fire, traffic, terrain, or aircraft damage.
Do not try to steer back onto the runway once you are off. After engine shutdown, nosewheel steering is gone, so any remaining directional control comes from braking only.
ISS mode selector to SOLO.
Install both seat safety pins before egress.
Set the parking brake as required and open the canopy if possible.

If the canopy cannot be opened or right-side egress is required, remove both CFS handle safety pins, rotate and pull both CFS handles, then release upper fittings, lower fittings, and leg restraint garters before exiting.
After the crew is clear, turn BAT, GEN, and AUX BAT OFF if time and situation allow.
Once clear of the aircraft, move away at a 45-degree angle off the tail and rally 300 feet from the aircraft while staying alert for emergency vehicles.

items.text: Warning-focused note: If the canopy fracturing system and canopy latch both fail, ejection may be the only remaining way out. Ensure oxygen mask on and visor down before actuating CFS.

sections.title: Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface / Emergency Ground Egress

items.text: Windshear should be avoided if possible, but once it is part of the picture the goal is to protect margin early instead of reacting late to the airspeed loss.

children.text: Treat thunderstorms, gust fronts, virga, LLWAS alerts, PIREPs, and recent frontal passages as cues to slow down the plan or avoid the approach or takeoff entirely.
Use the longest suitable runway, takeoff flaps, and delay rotation up to 10 knots above normal if windshear is suspected on takeoff.
After liftoff, maintain the proper climb attitude instead of chasing airspeed, and do not accelerate past normal climb speed until clear of the shear.
On approach, use takeoff flaps, fly up to 10 knots fast, and be stabilized by 1000 feet AGL.
If windshear is encountered on approach, execute an immediate go-around or waveoff.
Do not chase every airspeed change with large trim or power swings. Expect the wind gradient to change what the aircraft is doing as you descend.
Severe windshear is roughly a 15-knot airspeed change or 500 FPM vertical-speed change; that is your reminder to treat it as a real hazard, not a nuisance.

items.text: A UFCP failure is manageable, but it takes away the normal quick path for radio, nav, transponder, and baro changes. The fix is to transition calmly to the MFD NAV page and land as soon as practical.

children.text: First, check the UFCP circuit breaker and reset it if it is open.
Use ALT BARO on the NAV page to change the barometric setting, and ALT CNS to adjust COM, NAV, and transponder settings through the scratchpad and line-select keys.
From the frequency page you can also control transponder mode and altitude reporting without the UFCP.
The MFD NAV page is the backup path; these shortcuts are not available from the TSD page.

items.text: Know what you lose with the failure as well: FMS execute, Mag/True toggle, GS/CAS/TAS HUD speed toggle, and normal radio tuning through the UFCP are unavailable to the cockpit with the failed unit.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: The AOA approach is an energy-management pattern. Fly optimum AOA on downwind and through the 180 so pitch and power control the picture instead of chasing airspeed late.

children.text: After the climbout, level at pattern altitude on downwind at 120 KIAS.
Gear down, complete the Before Landing Checklist, and reduce power to about 15 to 20 percent.
Maintain about 3/4 to 1 wingtip distance from the runway while transitioning to on-speed AOA.
Flaps UP normally settles near 110 KIAS, flaps TO near 100 KIAS, and flaps LDG near 95 KIAS. Adjust pitch for 10.5 units / amber donut and use roughly 25 to 30 percent power to hold altitude.
Start the turn from the 180 with 15 to 20 percent power and a slight nose-low attitude.
Stay on-speed throughout the turn. If the green chevron appears, trim nose down and add power as required instead of forcing the aircraft around the corner.
A good checkpoint is about 450 feet AGL at the 90 and about 200 feet AGL, 1200 to 1500 feet from the threshold, on final.
Cross the threshold on-speed and fly it to a normal flare. The goal is an AOA approach to a flared landing, not an AOA touchdown.
Flaps LDG is the preferred setup because drag, camber, and engine response give the easiest on-speed picture.
Flaps TO is workable but gives less spool-up margin. Flaps UP is the hardest version and is the easiest way to create a high descent rate at low power.
Do not skid or slip the aircraft in the turn. Keep the airplane balanced and correct early with power and attitude instead of waiting until the flare.

items.text: Maneuvering speeds define the structural and control-input limits that protect the aircraft during aerobatic setup, recovery, and downhill acceleration.

children.text: VO is 227 KIAS. Above it, a full or abrupt control input in one axis can overstress the aircraft.
Full rudder above 150 KIAS exceeds rudder system limits and can damage the aircraft even if you are still below VO.
Watch the max airspeed of 316 KIAS / 0.67 Mach and the 19,020-foot Mach crossover whenever a recovery or downhill maneuver is accelerating.

items.text: Contact unusual attitudes are visual recoveries. The goal is to get back to controlled flight above 6000 feet AGL without turning a recoverable upset into OCF.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX.
Roll past 90 degrees AOB toward the nearest horizon, then use back stick to bring the nose to the horizon.
Roll upright as the nose approaches the horizon. If needed, allow the nose to fall slightly below the horizon to rebuild airspeed before returning to level flight.
Once the aircraft is flying again, roll wings level, raise the nose to level flight, check oil pressure, and set power as required.
Roll the aircraft to the nearest horizon while simultaneously retarding PCL to IDLE.
Use speed brake as required to help control the acceleration.
Make a smooth pull to level flight while monitoring airspeed up to 316 KIAS and performing AGSM as the G builds.
If AOA is below 18 units and airspeed is below 110 KIAS, you can advance power. If AOA is above 18 units or the airplane is not responding normally, transition to OCF recovery.
Roll the shortest way to the horizon.
Use power as required.
As the nose approaches or slightly passes the horizon, check and report oil pressure, then adjust power to maintain level flight.
Never push with forward stick in a nose-high recovery. That creates zero or negative G and can make the departure worse.
Avoid stopping the roll at knife-edge. Roll past 90 degrees and use positive G to bring the nose back to the horizon.
Stick shaker or buffet means the aircraft is at the edge of a stall. Reduce back pressure.
If the aircraft is stalled or in OCF, stop trying to fly a normal unusual-attitude recovery and go straight to OCF recovery.

items.text: An aileron roll is a 360-degree roll about the longitudinal axis. The nose traces a small circle around the horizon and the maneuver finishes on the entry heading.

children.text: Set about 80 percent PCL and enter at 180 to 220 KIAS.
Be at or above 6000 feet AGL, start wings level from upright flight, and use a clean heading or section-line reference before you begin the pull.
Complete the pre-stall / spin / aerobatic checks, clear the area, and confirm enough maneuvering room to recover on the entry heading.
Raise the nose smoothly to about 10 degrees nose high.
Relax back-stick pressure so the nose stops tracking upward, then apply full aileron in the desired direction.
Stay coordinated and neutralize aileron as the wings approach level so the maneuver finishes on the entry heading.
Finish wings level on the entry heading with altitude, airspeed, and nose attitude close enough that no cleanup turn or pitch correction is required.
Holding back stick through the roll drives the nose in an arc and makes the inverted portion ugly.
Waiting too long to start the roll bleeds energy and slows the roll rate.

items.text: The loop is a 360-degree turn in the vertical plane flown on a constant heading and nose track. Elevator is primary; rudder and aileron only keep the airplane coordinated and aligned.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX and enter at 230 to 250 KIAS.
Start wings level on a well-defined section line with clear airspace above, PSSA complete, and entry altitude reported over ICS.
Plan around 3000 feet of maneuvering room for the loop and recovery, and confirm you are high enough to finish without forcing the pull-out.
Initiate AGSM and make a smooth 4 G pull-up within about 2 to 3 seconds.
Keep the wings level with rudder, not aileron, and increase right rudder as airspeed decreases.
Expect roughly 100 to 120 KIAS over the top while maintaining positive G.
On the backside, let the nose fall, relax rudder as airspeed builds, resume AGSM, and recover wings level on the original heading.
Recover wings level on the original heading with energy back under control, enough altitude margin remaining, and no stall or OCF cues present.
A delayed pull-out is how you end up fast and low in the recovery.
If the aircraft stalls, go PCL IDLE, controls neutral, and let the nose fall to recover before trying to salvage the loop.

items.text: The half Cuban Eight is a modified loop that carries the airplane to a 45-degree nose-low line, then uses a half roll to recover upright, followed by a pull to finish on reciprocal heading at the original altitude.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX and enter at 230 to 250 KIAS.
Complete PSSA, clear the area, recheck wings level and the airspace above, and call the entry altitude over ICS.

Start wings level on a well-defined section line and allow roughly 3000 feet of maneuvering room so you can pull over the top, establish the 45-degree nose-low line, and still complete the pull-out on reciprocal heading.
Make the same smooth 4 G pull-up as the loop, keep the wings level with rudder, and do not use aileron through the pull.
Over the top, let the nose fall to the 45-degree nose-low line, then execute a coordinated roll upright.
After the roll, hold the 45-degree line long enough to look stable, then pull out on heading with energy under control.
Finish in level flight at entry airspeed on reciprocal heading, with the rollout and pull-out complete before you start cleaning up the picture.
Wrong G-loading or poor timing on the pull-up wrecks the picture early.
Aft stick during the roll drives an off-heading recovery.
Raising the nose too early after the roll erases the 45-degree line and turns the maneuver into a rushed pull-out.

items.text: The Immelmann is a half loop followed by a half roll to upright at the top. It should reverse your heading while keeping the airplane organized through the slowest part of the maneuver.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX and enter at 230 to 250 KIAS.
Start wings level on a well-defined section line, complete PSSA and clearing turns, and report the entry altitude over ICS.
Confirm clear airspace above before you begin the pull, because the top of the maneuver is slow and leaves little margin for rushed corrections.
Begin AGSM and make a smooth 4 G pull-up within about 2 to 3 seconds without aileron input, then keep the wings level with rudder as airspeed decays.
Past vertical, find the opposite horizon, use aileron to roll upright, and use slight forward stick past 90 degrees of roll if needed.
Let airspeed rebuild after the rollout without dropping the nose excessively or drifting off heading.
Finish upright and wings level on reciprocal heading, slightly nose high, around 120 KIAS, ready to let airspeed rebuild without an avoidable descent.
Poor rudder coordination shows up fast at the top of the maneuver.
Rolling too early or too late creates off-heading or nose-low recoveries.
Pulling during the roll is an easy way to ruin the heading reversal.

items.text: A Split-S combines a half roll to inverted with the second half of a loop. It reverses direction while converting altitude into airspeed and finishes in level flight.

children.text: Retard PCL to IDLE, hold altitude, and slow to about 140 KIAS after transitioning through 150 KIAS.
Start from wings-level upright flight with PSSA complete, the area cleared, and enough altitude for about 3000 feet of altitude loss.
Raise the nose to about 10 degrees nose high, then execute a half roll to inverted and confirm the wings are truly level before you pull.
Apply back stick to pull through the horizon while maximizing nose track without stalling.
If you get shaker or buffet, ease off the back stick rather than forcing the pull-through.
As airspeed and G build, perform AGSM, recover to level flight, check and report oil pressure, and add power as required.
Finish in level flight on reciprocal heading with oil pressure checked, power reset as required, and enough altitude margin left to reset cleanly.
Solos are prohibited from Split-S, Immelmann, Combination Maneuvers, and sustained inverted flight.
Ensure the wings are level inverted before the pull. Use a ground reference above the canopy bow to keep the pull straight.
If the aircraft becomes unresponsive during the pull-through, stop trying to force the maneuver and transition to OCF recovery.

items.text: A wingover is flown as two leafs, each a smooth 180-degree reversal combining a climbing turn and a descending turn. The full series returns the aircraft to the original heading at approximately the original altitude and airspeed.

children.text: Set about 70 percent PCL and enter at 200 to 220 KIAS.
Start from level flight with the area cleared, PSSA complete, and enough altitude to work the nose-low backside safely.
Pick a reference point about 90 degrees off the wingtip and be ready to fly the maneuver as a pair so you return to original heading after the second leaf.
Begin with a shallow bank and let nose position and bank angle build together.
As the nose approaches the horizon on the climbing side, expect bank to build toward the steepest part of the maneuver.
Let the nose fall and time the roll so the airplane finishes wings level on reciprocal heading without a rushed pull at the bottom.
Finish the first wingover on reciprocal heading at original altitude and approximately entry airspeed, then repeat opposite direction and end back on original heading without a rushed recovery.
Rushing the maneuver makes the bank and pitch get out of sync.
Exceeding 90 degrees of bank or forcing the recovery is a sign the setup picture was not right.
If you are off airspeed, altitude, or heading at the end, the timing was not smooth enough.

items.text: A barrel roll is a 360-degree rolling maneuver flown around an imaginary reference point about 45 degrees off the nose. Pitch and roll are blended so the nose traces a corkscrew path and the aircraft returns to the original heading and altitude.

children.text: Set about 80 percent PCL and enter at 200 to 220 KIAS.
Complete PSSA, clear the area, report entry altitude, and pick the 45-degree off-the-nose reference point before you move the stick.
Start straight and level so the roll begins from a stable sight picture instead of from a wandering heading or altitude.
Raise the nose smoothly with the wings level, then begin the coordinated pull-and-roll around the reference.
Be wings level while inverted at the 90-degree checkpoint and finish on the original heading and altitude.
Keep positive G throughout and avoid flying it like an instrument maneuver from inside the cockpit.
Finish on original heading and altitude with wings level, positive G maintained throughout, and a symmetrical path above and below the horizon.
Poor pitch-and-roll coordination turns the barrel roll into either an aileron roll or a lopsided climbing turn.
Bad rudder inputs create imbalance and make the path asymmetrical above and below the horizon.

items.text: Out-of-control flight recovery starts with recognition, disciplined neutral-control recovery inputs, and patience while the aircraft responds.

children.text: Poststall gyration shows up right after the stall with uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high AOA, and controls that feel ineffective.
An incipient spin is the transition between poststall gyration and a steady-state spin. Expect oscillatory spin-like motion, a pegged turn needle, stalled AOA, and changing airspeed.
A steady-state spin has aerodynamic and inertial forces in balance. Expect the turn needle pegged and airspeed around 120 to 135 KIAS, stable or only slightly oscillating.
Airspeed and nose attitude are not reliable stall cues here. Better cues are uncommanded pitch-up, nose drop, wing roll, or pitch bucking.
Go PCL IDLE, physically confirm controls neutral, check altitude, and then recover from the resulting unusual attitude once the stall breaks and the airplane responds.
If the aircraft is not responding yet, keep the controls neutral and do not start inventing anti-spin inputs early just because the motion feels wrong.
Time distortion and G distortion are part of the trap. Be patient and let the recovery work before you decide it has failed.
6000 feet AGL is the minimum altitude for uncontrolled ejection.

items.text: Airborne damaged aircraft procedures apply once the aircraft is still controllable but structural, control-surface, or engine damage is suspected.

children.text: Maintain aircraft control first.
If the aircraft is uncontrollable, eject.
Assess engine status. If bird strike or damage is suspected within the prop arc, be ready to execute a PEL.

If the aircraft is still controllable, perform a controllability check for structural or flight-control damage and, if practical, climb to at least 6500 feet AGL before working the rest of the problem.
Slow the aircraft progressively while checking flight characteristics, test the power range, and avoid stalling or using full control inputs to maintain flight.
If flap damage is known or suspected, do not reposition flaps once the configuration risk is identified.
Fly no slower than minimum controllable airspeed plus 20 KIAS until final, and plan a power-on straight-in approach with minimum flare.
Limited rudder or crosswind problems may require a no-flap straight-in, slow PCL movement on a go-around, and differential braking during rollout.

items.text: Combination maneuvers are an energy-management and planning problem as much as they are a stick-and-rudder problem. The goal is to make the sequence look deliberate instead of like a set of disconnected recoveries.

children.text: Choose and brief the sequence before you start, including maneuver order, expected heading changes, and the altitude and energy state you need when each maneuver ends.
Start with enough working altitude and airspeed to fly the highest-energy maneuver first without painting yourself into a slow or low corner.
Use the normal clear-area, checklist, and working-area setup before the first maneuver so the sequence starts from a controlled picture instead of a rushed one.
Fly the sequence as one continuous evolution, but transition while the previous maneuver is still under control instead of waiting to think about the next step after the recovery.
Maintain positive aircraft control and keep the outside picture primary so heading, altitude, and energy changes stay ahead of you.
If the first maneuver ends sloppy, recover to level flight and reset instead of forcing a bad second maneuver.
The final maneuver ends on the planned heading, altitude, and airspeed with enough control margin to recover or re-enter the next profile without rescue coaching.
Poor maneuver sequencing is the fastest way to create avoidable low-energy or low-altitude problems.
Do not let a sloppy first maneuver force you into a rushed transition that makes the rest of the sequence worse.

items.text: Treat the HUD as a heads-up cross-check for aerobatic setup and recovery, not as the primary thing you are trying to fly off of. It should support the outside picture and help you stay oriented when the workload jumps.

children.text: Know the basic job of the HUD: it presents flight, navigation, steering, and master-mode information in front of the pilot, with the repeater available in the other cockpit.
Understand what Flash, Limit Cross, and invalid or missing symbology are telling you so you do not chase a cue that is outside the field of view or no longer trustworthy.
For AOA work, the HUD should help confirm the on-speed picture and the basic attitude cues, but it should not pull your scan inside during the pattern.

For aerobatics, use the HUD to support section-line awareness, pitch / bank orientation, and quick cross-checks like the aerobatic maneuver chart or SSR references while keeping the horizon and outside attitude picture primary.
For unusual attitudes or OCF-related work, the HUD is a secondary orientation tool once you have re-anchored to the correct recovery picture; it is not a substitute for flying the recovery.
You should be able to explain the broad HUD cues that matter in this event without trying to brief every symbol on the combiner glass.
If the symbology stops making sense, look outside, regain the correct attitude picture, and then use the HUD as a confirming cross-check again.

items.text: OCF Recovery and Airborne Damaged Aircraft

events.overview: This review sim checks whether you can brief the local-flying framework without leaning on memorized place names. Be ready to explain how to study the sectional, how outlying-field entries and departures are sequenced, and what must always be confirmed from the current published procedure before you launch or recover.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM6101 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Local course rules are the unit's contract for how traffic is deconflicted, where training aircraft are expected to be, and what altitudes, speeds, and reporting habits keep the area predictable. The goal is not to memorize one field's nickname map forever; it is to know how to brief and verify the current local procedure.

children.text: Know the entry gates, altitude blocks, speed expectations, noise-sensitive areas, and any restricted routes or solo limitations that apply to the day's sortie.
Be ready to brief which agency owns the handoff at each phase of arrival or departure and when the route changes from a general course-rule transit into a specific field-recovery procedure.
If weather, gear, flap, or traffic issues make the normal route unrealistic, ask early for the direct recovery or alternate entry that the current procedure allows.
The current published procedure, day-of brief, and controlling agencies decide the actual route names, gates, and reporting points.
Do not study course rules as a string of local proper nouns with no logic behind them. Study the purpose of each leg and then verify the local labels before flight.

items.text: OLF operations are about disciplined pattern entry, positive communication, and a willingness to discontinue early if the sequencing picture is not clean. The field may be remote, but the expectations should still feel methodical.

children.text: Know the authorized entry options for the field of use, the initial point geometry, and which agency or CTAF flow is used to determine runway, pattern traffic, and whether the field is saturated.

If the field does not answer, traffic cannot be sorted, or the runway/pattern picture is not what you expected by the published decision point, execute the discontinued entry instead of pressing inward to solve it late.
Pattern priority belongs to the aircraft already established correctly in the pattern or break, not to the one trying to force its way in with a late call.
Depart only when you are number one and clear of conflicts, then fly the published departure geometry before accelerating, climbing, or turning farther onto course.
If the field uses a remote operator or crash-crew radio concept, treat that as a field-specific comm layer to verify from the day's brief, not as a universal aviation norm.
The real study standard is being able to explain when you continue a normal pattern, when you reset to initial, and when you leave entirely to rebuild the picture.

items.text: Home-field arrival is the transition from area navigation back into terminal sequencing. The details are local, but the logic is transferable: arrive at the correct gate, at the correct energy, already knowing what kind of recovery you are asking for.

children.text: Know the authorized arrival families, the expected arrival altitude and airspeed profile, and the common reporting point where you transition from course rules to tower sequencing.
If you are requesting a straight-in or direct recovery because of weather, traffic, or abnormal configuration, say so early enough that Approach and Tower can build the correct plan around you.
Once inside the terminal area, configure below the correct airspeed gates, complete the landing checks on time, and be ready to report the entry or base/final call the local procedure expects.
The specific named routes, bridges, shoreline references, and reporting-point labels belong to the current local procedure.
What matters in the brief is understanding the arrival gate, the sequencing point, and the recovery options if the standard arrival stops fitting the actual situation.

items.text: How to study it without local leakage:

A local VFR sectional review should prove that you can use the chart to build situational awareness before you start flying local nicknames by memory. The sectional is how you verify where the field, checkpoints, obstacles, airspace, and alternate options really are.

children.text: Be able to identify the major class airspace boundaries, field elevations, runway orientation, prominent checkpoints, obstacle concentrations, and MEF along the local training routes.
Know which nearby airports are realistic alternates, what special-use or noise-sensitive areas matter, and where the chart warns you that navigation by assumption becomes risky.
Use the chart to cross-check local course-rule descriptions instead of trusting memory when the weather, runway, or traffic picture changes.

items.text: What to review on the chart:

children.text: If the sectional review cannot answer where you are, what airspace you are entering, or what the nearest safe divert is, then the review is too shallow.
This item is not about owning one hometown map forever. It is about knowing how to extract the right information from the chart at any local training base.

studyNotes.summary: Brief the local-flying framework in a transferable way: chart first, course-rule logic second, then field entry and recovery specifics from the current procedure.

events.title: Course Rules, OLF Operations, and Arrival Review

events.overview: This review sim is about judgment before the airplane ever gets busy. Be ready to brief IMSAFE, CRM, see and avoid discipline, weather and cloud-clearance judgment, and the chart knowledge that keeps those decisions tied to real airspace and terrain instead of habit.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM6102 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: IMSAFE is the personal go/no-go screen that should happen before every event, not a rescue card you pull after poor planning catches up to you. If one of the categories is red, the right answer is to surface it early and honestly.

children.text: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, and Eating all affect judgment, attention, and tolerance for workload.
The checklist applies to any training event, not just a flight in the aircraft.
If you are not fit to train, tell the instructor and duty chain immediately instead of trying to negotiate with yourself in the brief.
IMSAFE is not a loophole for being unprepared or late. It is a safety tool for identifying real human-factor risk.
The follow-on conversation should be professional and honest. The goal is to protect training quality and safety, not to punish someone for speaking up.

items.text: CRM is the use of defined behavioral skills to reduce preventable errors, maximize crew coordination, and improve risk management from before the brief until after the debrief. In primary training that means both the IP and SNA are actively protecting the cockpit, even though the student is still learning to think like a single-seat pilot.

children.text: Decision making: choose a sound course of action based on the actual facts, not pride or momentum.
Assertiveness: speak up professionally and keep speaking until the concern is understood.
Mission analysis: plan the short-term, long-term, and contingency versions of the event.
Communication, leadership, adaptability, and situational awareness all support the same goal: a cockpit where errors are caught early instead of cleaned up late.
Good CRM does not remove student responsibility. It improves safety while the student is still expected to think ahead and fly the aircraft.
In a fast-developing problem, clear communication and role clarity usually matter more than a perfect explanation.

items.text: How it shows up in primary:

See and avoid is still the primary VFR defense against a midair collision. The lesson is not simply 'look outside more'; it is understanding how human vision fails and building a scan that works before traffic becomes urgent.

children.text: Most midair collisions occur in daylight, in VMC, within about five miles of an airport, and often in crossing or overtaking situations.
Accommodation delay means your eyes need time to refocus from the cockpit to outside traffic.
Empty-field myopia, narrow focus, blossom effect, glare, haze, and cluttered backgrounds all make real traffic harder to see than students expect.
Build a comfortable scan about 60 degrees either side of center and about 10 degrees up and down, while still clearing the rest of the area.
Use TCAS to help point your eyes, but do not replace the VFR visual scan with the display.
If a collision threat is immediate, displace the aircraft from its current flight path first. Collision avoidance outranks overstress concerns in that moment.

items.text: Cloud clearances are a judgment item, not just a legal trivia item. The point is to know the VMC margin you actually need for the airspace, altitude, and training task you are flying, then apply any unit restrictions that are more conservative than the baseline rules.

children.text: Know the published VFR weather minimums and cloud-clearance requirements that apply to the airspace you expect to use.
Understand that training-command or local SOP restrictions may be tighter than the bare legal minimums, especially for contact work, solo events, or outlying-field operations.
If the visibility or cloud picture is forcing you to invent workarounds, you are already in a judgment problem.
This item is best answered by explaining how you determine whether a VFR route, altitude, or pattern is still legal and still smart.
Do not answer with one unit's local weather rule and assume that equals the full concept.

items.text: The local VFR sectional review should prove you can read the chart in a way that supports risk management. This is where chart literacy meets weather, traffic, airspace, and diversion planning.

children.text: Review the sectional legend, class airspace, prominent visual checkpoints, obstacle and MEF symbology, common frequencies, and likely divert fields.
Use the chart to answer practical questions: where can I stay VFR, what airspace am I about to enter, and what is my nearest safe alternate if the weather or traffic picture changes.
Treat the chart as a planning and verification tool, not a prop you glance at only after getting lost.
A strong answer connects the sectional to actual judgment: airspace, terrain, weather margins, traffic concentration, and route flexibility.
A weak answer turns this into a memorized local arrival instead of a chart-reading discussion item.

studyNotes.summary: Treat this as a judgment brief: IMSAFE, CRM, see and avoid discipline, weather margins, and chart literacy all need to reinforce each other.

events.title: Risk Management and VFR Judgment
