events.overview: This sortie is about crosswind control first and recovery discipline second. You should be able to brief how the wind changes the takeoff, approach, and landing picture, then keep normal unusual-attitude recoveries clearly separated from OCF so a bad upset does not get worse.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4104 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Crosswind work is one continuous control problem from lineup through rollout. The big mistake is treating takeoff, final, and landing as separate moments instead of one uninterrupted wind-correction picture.

children.text: Before lineup, note wind direction and gusts from tower and the windsock so the first control input is anticipated instead of reactive.
Hold positive aileron into the wind once in position for takeoff. Use up to full deflection at the start of the roll, then relax aileron as speed builds to keep the wings level at liftoff.
Use rudder to stop weather-vaning and keep the nose on centerline. A left crosswind can add to the aircraft's normal left-yaw tendency, so expect to need even more right rudder.
Rotate firmly at 90 KIAS, or add half the gust factor up to 10 knots in gusty conditions, and let the aircraft fly off instead of forcing it into a skip.
Once safely airborne, level the wings, allow the aircraft to crab into the wind, and confirm the ball is centered.
Crab into the wind on downwind to hold the correct track and wingtip distance.

Overshooting winds increase groundspeed in the final turn and usually require slightly more bank with slightly lower power. Undershooting winds usually require slightly less bank with slightly higher power.
Start the final turn with about 30 degrees AOB. Do not exceed 45 degrees of bank; if more is required to make final, wave off.
After rollout on final, use aileron to hold extended centerline, rudder to align the aircraft with the runway, and extra power as required to overcome the drag from cross-controls.
In gusty conditions, add half the gust factor to final approach speed, up to a 10-knot increase.
Transition to the wing-low method on final and keep the upwind wing down through the flare. Do not level the wings prior to touchdown.
Use rudder to align the longitudinal axis with the runway and increase aileron into the wind as airspeed decreases and the controls become less effective.
Touch down on the upwind main first with zero side motion. A crab or drift at touchdown can start a swerve and runway departure.

On a full stop, keep feeding aileron into the wind during rollout, maintain directional control with rudder and brakes, and do not aggressively yank the aircraft back to centerline if touchdown started slightly off-center.
On a touch-and-go, hold the crosswind inputs on the deck, apply positive rotation at flying speed, then level the wings and let the aircraft crab into the wind once safely airborne.
Skipping on takeoff usually means the upwind wing started flying early because the aileron picture or rotation was wrong.
If proper crosswind control is not in before touchdown, or if an uncontrollable drift develops in the flare or after touchdown, wave off.
Do not let brake use or centerline fixation distract you from the real priority: keep the airplane aligned and the upwind wing under control.

items.text: Out-of-control flight starts when the aircraft is stalled and no longer responding like normal flight. The recovery only works if you recognize what phase you are in and stop trying to fly it like an unusual attitude.

children.text: Post-stall gyrations show up as uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high or stalled AOA, and controls that feel ineffective or reversed.
An incipient spin looks like oscillatory spin-like motion with stalled AOA, a fully deflected turn needle, and airspeed moving toward the steady-state value. Expect about two turns in this phase.
A steady-state spin stabilizes around 120-135 KIAS with the turn needle pegged in the spin direction, 18+ units AOA, and roughly 400-500 feet of altitude loss per turn.
Airspeed and nose attitude are poor stall cues here. Better cues are uncommanded pitch-up, nose drop, wing roll-off, or pitch bucking.

For post-stall gyrations and incipient spin, go PCL IDLE, physically confirm controls neutral, check altitude, and recover from the resulting unusual attitude once the stall breaks and the aircraft responds.
Be patient with neutral controls. Starting anti-spin guesses too early can make the departure worse.

If the aircraft is in a steady-state erect spin, use NATOPS erect-spin recovery logic: identify spin direction, apply full opposite rudder, move the stick forward of neutral, keep ailerons neutral, and hold the inputs until rotation stops before recovering from the resulting unusual attitude.
If gear or flaps are down during an unintentional spin, retract them immediately to protect against airspeed-limit damage.
A normal unusual-attitude recovery does not fix a stalled or departed aircraft. If the aircraft condition is in doubt, go directly to OCF recovery.
Physically neutral stick matters more than trimmed neutral.
If OCF continues into an unrecoverable rapid descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Contact unusual attitudes are visual recoveries. The goal is to get back to controlled flight above 6000 feet AGL without creating a stall, accelerated stall, or OCF in the process.

children.text: Set PCL to MAX as required in low-airspeed situations.
Roll past 90 degrees AOB toward the nearest horizon and use back stick to bring the nose down to it.
Roll upright as the nose approaches the horizon. If the airspeed is very low, allow the nose to fall slightly below the horizon before rolling fully upright so the controls come alive again.
Once the aircraft is responding normally, roll wings level, raise the nose to level flight, check oil pressure, and set power as required.
Roll to the nearest horizon while simultaneously retarding PCL to IDLE.
Use speed brake as required and make a smooth pull to level flight while respecting the 316-KIAS limit and performing AGSM.
If AOA is below 18 units and airspeed is very low, you can advance power. If AOA is above 18 units or the aircraft is not responding normally, transition to OCF recovery.
Roll the shortest way to the horizon.
Use power as required.
As the nose approaches or slightly passes the horizon, check and report oil pressure, then adjust power to maintain level flight.
Never push the nose over with forward stick in a nose-high recovery. That creates zero or negative G and can deepen the problem.
Avoid stopping the roll at knife-edge. Rolling past 90 degrees and using positive G is the expeditious recovery method.
Stick shaker or buffet means you are near a stall. Reduce back pressure.
If the aircraft is stalled or in OCF, stop trying to fly a normal unusual-attitude recovery and go straight to OCF recovery.

studyNotes.summary: Brief the wind and the recovery logic before the airplane gets busy: crosswind corrections never stop, unusual-attitude recoveries stay clean, and anything stalled or out of control goes straight to OCF recovery.

events.overview: This sortie is the bridge from normal contact flying into engine and emergency-landing decision making. Be ready to brief the limits that matter, the PT6/PMU logic behind the indications you see, and the differences between an ELP, a PEL, and a forced landing when time and energy are running out.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4201 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Know the limits you are most likely to brief, violate, or use to decide whether the aircraft is still being flown normally. This is not a memorization contest for every number in NATOPS; it is about knowing the ones that change your go/no-go and landing decisions.

children.text: Maximum ramp weight is 6950 pounds. Maximum takeoff and landing weight are 6900 pounds. Maximum zero fuel weight is 5850 pounds.
Maximum baggage-compartment weight is 80 pounds.
Ground operation is limited to ambient temperatures from -23 C to +43 C.
Maximum touchdown rate is 600 FPM when the mains are serviced to 185 +/- 5 PSI, and 780 FPM when they are serviced to 225 +/- 5 PSI.
Those landing-rate numbers matter because a low-energy ELP or forced landing can tempt you into accepting a sink rate that damages the aircraft.
Do not open the canopy on the ground with surface winds above 40 knots.
Ejection-seat occupant limits are approximately 131.8 to 279.4 pounds including equipment and flight gear.

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full NATOPS-style engine brief. For this event, be able to connect the PT6A-68, PMU, and propeller system to the cues that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

children.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine engine, so the gas-generator section can still be healthy while the propeller side is the part misbehaving.
The PMU normally schedules fuel, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response. Weight-on-wheels logic gives you about 60-61% N1 on the ground and about 67% N1 in flight.
The reduction gearbox and propeller interface logic are why NP, torque, and thrust can change even when the gas-generator section has not completely failed.
Healthy N1 with abnormal NP or torque should make you think propeller or control logic before you call it a total engine failure.
Loss of oil pressure or hydraulic pressure together with rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT is a much stronger engine-failure picture.
If the PMU drops offline or is selected OFF, fuel scheduling becomes manual and the workload jumps immediately, especially during landing or restart decisions.
Do not casually lift the PCL cutoff gate in flight. Mishaps have happened from inadvertent shutdown attempts.
Once ST READY extinguishes, the automatic start protections are gone, so any PMU OFF or manual-fuel work demands tighter monitoring.
Starts with PMU OFF are not recommended, and any event that leaves you in manual mode should immediately change how cautious you are with throttle movement and landing rollout planning.

items.text: Engine malfunctions are easier to manage when you stop chasing a single annunciator and instead build a full picture from power, N1, torque, ITT, NP, oil pressure, and hydraulic pressure.

children.text: A flameout usually gives you rapid loss of power and airspeed, rapidly decaying N1, torque, and ITT, loss of oil and hydraulic pressure, and the propeller moving toward feather.
An engine seizure can look similar, but often drives oil and hydraulic pressure to zero more abruptly and may include a CHIP warning.

A rollback is an uncommanded power reduction, often from PMU scheduling problems. If the PMU stays online, fuel flow and N1 may simply be lower than expected; if it drops offline, you may get a step change in power.
Uncommanded propeller feather usually shows up as reduced NP, increased torque, more prop noise, less thrust, and sometimes vibration.
A good quick discriminator is whether N1 is still healthy while torque or NP are not. That points you toward prop-system logic rather than a full engine failure.
High-value red warnings for this event are PMU FAIL, FUEL PX, OIL PX, CHIP, CHK ENG, GEN BUS, and BATT BUS.
PMU STATUS in flight matters because it can leave you at flight idle on landing and change the rollout picture.
Do not memorize every amber or white advisory for this event. Focus on the engine indications that change whether you continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

items.text: The emergency landing pattern is the geometry you use for both a PEL and a forced landing. The profile is the same; the difference is whether power is still available and how you correct a low-energy state.

children.text: Interception is normally at high key, 3000 feet AGL, with 2500 feet AGL as the minimum high-key intercept.
Think of the profile in checkpoints: high key at 3000 feet AGL, low key at 1500 feet AGL, base key at 600-800 feet AGL, and final at 110 KIAS minimum.
Maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final. Do not trade airspeed away just to hit an altitude number.
Best glide clean is about 125 KIAS with roughly 1350-1500 FPM sink and about 2 nautical miles of glide for every 1000 feet lost.
With the gear down and clean otherwise, best glide is about 105 KIAS and glide ratio drops to about 1.6 nautical miles per 1000 feet lost.
Use winds, runway suitability, field elevation, and actual energy state to decide whether you can reach high key, low key, or need another option.

ORM 3-2-1 drives the low-altitude decision chain: do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing scenario unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver safely to land.
At 300 feet AGL you make the final continue-or-eject decision, at 200 feet the gear should be confirmed down, and at 100 feet the aircraft should be on centerline.
If the profile is falling apart, do not delay the wave-off in training or the eject decision in the real event.
A high-energy state is fixed with methods like 360s, bow ties, S-turns, slips, or early drag, but every choice should still preserve a predictable arrival at high key.
The primary reference in the ELP is the runway. Crosscheck actual position and energy against the next checkpoint early enough to make a smooth correction.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual forced-landing situation unless the runway is in sight, you are on profile, and you can still maneuver safely to land.
Allowing the aircraft to get slow to hit altitude checkpoints is dangerous; maintain 120 KIAS minimum until intercepting final and 110 KIAS minimum on final.
Treat ORM 3-2-1 and the final continue/eject gate as hard warning-and-caution discipline, not as flexible guidelines.

items.text: A PEL is for an engine problem where power still exists but failure may be imminent. The student trap is treating it like a routine recovery and burning up the engine's remaining time with slow procedures or excessive troubleshooting.

children.text: The memory aid is Turn, Climb/Accelerate, Clean, Check, BIP, Determine, Deliver, Reduce, Lower, Report.
Turn toward the nearest suitable field immediately. Then climb at 140 KIAS to DEGA or accelerate to build energy if a climb is not appropriate.
Clean the aircraft as soon as practical because extra drag kills climb and glide performance.
Check for secondary indications and use boost pump and ignition as required.
Do not blindly select boost pump or ignition on if an airstart would not be warranted after a failure, such as oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
Determine the runway before intercepting the profile and deliver the ISPI report early enough that everyone else understands your plan.
Reduce to 4-6% torque no sooner than DEGA.
Lower the gear no later than high key, fly 120 KIAS minimum on profile, lower flaps no sooner than low key, and use power immediately to fix a low-energy state.
Inside base key, use normal power corrections to ensure a safe and controlled landing instead of preserving some imaginary perfect emergency picture.
Time is the critical resource in many PELs. Do not turn an impending engine failure into an actual one by being slow.
On a PEL, never accept being below profile prior to the actual point on the ground. Power is available, so use it.
If a safe landing becomes unlikely, the answer is not to keep troubleshooting. Commit to the next safe option.

items.text: A forced landing is what happens when power is gone or insufficient for continued flight and the airplane has enough energy to reach a suitable hard-surface landing area. If that energy or runway picture is not there, the answer becomes eject, not hope.

children.text: The first memory items are Zoom/Glide 125 KIAS minimum, PCL OFF, intercept the ELP, and attempt an airstart only if warranted.
Do not attempt an airstart if the failure involves oil-system malfunction, chip light, fire light, or FOD.
If an airstart is not warranted, pull the firewall shutoff handle and commit to either the forced landing or ejection decision.
Use the nearest suitable hard-surface field of adequate length and align the aircraft with the landing direction as early as possible.
If you cannot reach high key, intercept the ELP at another point with the proper configuration and airspeed rather than stretching the glide into a bad setup.
At low key, use flaps only if energy supports it. If the airplane is not on profile approaching base key, eject in the real event or wave off in the simulated one.
Do not descend below 2000 feet AGL in an actual engine-failure case unless you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to maneuver to land.
Maintain 110 KIAS minimum on final until the landing transition. Anticipate a longer flare with 4-6% torque simulating a feathered prop.
If touchdown will occur past the first one-third of the runway in a simulated event, wave off. In the actual event, do not delay the eject decision once safe landing is unlikely.
Air-starts are not recommended below 2000 feet AGL because the primary task there is either safe recovery or ejection.
A flamed-out engine at 125 KIAS typically shows 0% indicated N1, torque near zero, and may still show a small residual oil-pressure indication.
Do not dissipate energy casually in a real forced landing. Use the time you have to build the safest runway plan possible.

items.text: Aldis lamp signals matter when the radios are gone and the tower still has to control you. The student value here is not just the colors; it is knowing how to acknowledge them and how they change your immediate action.

children.text: On the ground: steady green means cleared to take off, flashing green means cleared to taxi, steady red means stop, flashing red means taxi clear of runway, flashing white means return to starting point, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.

In flight: steady green means cleared to land, flashing green means return for landing, steady red means give way and continue circling, flashing red means do not land, and alternating red/green means exercise extreme caution.
A red pyrotechnic signal in flight means do not land and wave off immediately regardless of previous instructions.
Acknowledge in daytime with aileron or rudder movement on the ground and wing rocking in the air.
At night, acknowledge by flashing aircraft lights.

studyNotes.summary: Know the limits, understand what the engine and PMU are telling you, and commit early to the right landing-option chain before a manageable malfunction turns into an actual engine-failure problem.

events.summary: NATOPS limits, PT6/PMU basics, and the ELP-to-PEL-to-forced-landing decision chain.

items.text: Start with the big picture, then walk the air path, then the fuel path, and only then talk about cockpit indications. That flow makes the brief sound like you understand the engine instead of reciting disconnected parts.

children.text: Purpose: convert fuel and air into shaft horsepower for the propeller while supplying the accessory and lubrication systems that keep the engine alive.
Architecture: free-turbine, reverse-flow engine with separate gas-generation and power sections.
Briefing payoff: once you understand where power is made and how the propeller is controlled, engine-failure indications make a lot more sense.

items.text: The PT6A-68 is a free-turbine turboprop flat-rated to produce 1100 shaft horsepower. It is a reverse-flow design with two independent sections.

children.text: Gas-generation section: four-stage axial compressor, single-stage centrifugal compressor, combustion chamber, and single-stage compressor turbine.
Power section: two-stage axial-flow power turbine, exhaust case, and reduction gearbox.
The power turbine is not mechanically linked to the compressor. That is why the engine can still be producing gas-generator indications even when the propeller side is degrading.
The reduction gearbox takes turbine speed of roughly 30,000 RPM down to about 2000 RPM at the Hartzell four-blade constant-speed propeller.
The engine is cooled and lubricated by a dedicated oil system, and the engine data manager monitors the operating parameters that drive the EICAS messages you brief.
The accessory-drive section powers the engine-driven components that keep the engine, oil, and propeller-control systems functioning.

items.text: The air molecule brief is the easiest way to explain how the PT6 makes power: trace the air from the intake to the exhaust and explain what each section is doing to it.

children.text: Inlet air travels rearward through the intake duct and inertial separator, which helps throw debris and moisture out of the airstream.
The air then moves forward through the four-stage axial compressor and the single-stage centrifugal compressor. The diffuser slows that flow and converts velocity into static pressure.
Diffused air passes through straightening vanes before it mixes with atomized fuel in the combustion chamber.
The expanding gas first drives the single-stage compressor turbine, which is mechanically linked to the compressor and keeps the gas-generator cycle going.
That same gas then drives the separate two-stage power turbine, which turns the reduction gearbox through its own shaft.
Exhaust gases leave through the stacks and add a small amount of thrust, but the real output the pilot cares about is the shaft power being delivered to the propeller.

items.text: The fuel molecule brief should explain how the engine meters fuel rather than just saying fuel goes to the nozzles.

children.text: Fuel leaves the tanks and reaches the engine fuel pump and fuel-management unit, where it is metered based on PCL position and system inputs.
Metered fuel is sent through the flow divider to the fuel nozzles, where it is atomized into the compressed air inside the combustion chamber.
During start, the igniters light the mixture. Once the engine is running, combustion becomes self-sustaining.
The PMU and related control logic are why fuel scheduling, acceleration, deceleration, and propeller response feel coordinated in normal operations.

Mounted around the reduction gearbox are the chip detector, PIU, torque probe, and PMA, which is why a gearbox or propeller-control problem can change what the fuel and power picture looks like from the cockpit.
If you can explain how the FMU, PMU, and propeller-control pieces interact, you are much better prepared to talk through rollback, feather, or PMU-related malfunctions.

events.overview: This sortie is about understanding what the hydraulic system buys you before you go spin, OCF, and crosswind work. Be ready to brief the hydraulic system well enough to explain normal versus emergency services, then keep the spin, OCF, anti-spin, and crosswind boundaries straight once the aircraft departs normal flight.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4202 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full hydraulic walk-through. For this event, know what hydraulic power you are counting on in normal flight, what changes when the normal system is lost, and which indications change your gear, flap, or NWS decisions.

children.text: Normal hydraulic power runs the landing gear, TO/LDG flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
The engine-driven pump maintains roughly 3000 +/- 120 PSI from a 5-quart reservoir. That normal-system pressure is what you are relying on anytime you move gear, flaps, or speed brake.
Think normal versus emergency: the power package and selector manifold do the routine work, and the emergency accumulator gives you one backup shot if the main system is gone.
HYDR FL LO points you toward a fluid-quantity, leak, or normal-system problem and should make you stop assuming normal gear or flap operation is guaranteed.
EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO suggests a leak or hydraulic-fuse problem and a thinner backup margin.
Emergency gear extension leaves the inboard doors extended, and emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector but the flaps cannot be retracted once they are out.
Disengage NWS before sharp turns that require differential braking.
Do not take off with a known NWS problem; centering issues can create takeoff or landing control problems.
If the emergency accumulator has been discharged for maintenance, the related caution should be out before flight.

items.text: The spin is not a finesse maneuver. It is a deliberate stalled-yaw entry used to teach recognition, orientation, and disciplined recovery once the aircraft departs normal flight.

children.text: Trim the aircraft in slow cruise at 150 KIAS.
Minimum entry altitude is 13,500 feet AGL. Enter below 22,000 feet pressure altitude and recover before 10,000 feet pressure altitude.
The entry is built to begin with PCL going to IDLE before the nose comes up; do not build the pitch picture first and pull power late.
Perform the Pre-Stalling, Spinning, and Aerobatic Checklist and clear the area thoroughly, including TCAS as appropriate.
Check wings level, retard PCL to IDLE, and smoothly raise the nose to about 30 degrees above the horizon.
At the stick shaker, lead the stall with slight rudder in the desired spin direction.
When the aircraft stalls and the nose pitches down, smoothly apply full rudder in the direction of spin and full back stick with ailerons neutral.
Call out altitude, AOA, airspeed, and turn-needle direction so the phase of the spin stays clear.
The maneuver is complete when the IP-directed recovery is finished, oil pressure is checked and reported normal, and the aircraft is back in controlled flight inside the working area.
Raising the nose before PCL is fully at IDLE.
Letting disorientation delay recognition or recovery.
Failing to neutralize controls as rotation stops or pulling too aggressively into a secondary stall.
Spins are flown clean. If gear or flaps are down in an unintentional spin, get them up immediately to avoid airspeed-limit damage.
Ailerons remain neutral throughout intentional spin training.
Silence the gear-warning horn before entry so it does not interfere with recognition calls.

items.text: OCF recovery procedures are for post-stall gyrations and incipient spins where the aircraft has departed normal flight but has not yet stabilized into a true steady-state spin.

children.text: Post-stall gyration shows up as uncommanded motion about one or more axes, erratic airspeed, high or stalled AOA, and controls that feel ineffective or wrong.
An incipient spin shows stalled AOA, a fully deflected turn needle, and airspeed changing toward the steady-state value. Expect about the first two turns here.
If you are not yet in a stabilized 120-135 KIAS, 18+ units AOA, steady-state picture, stay with OCF recovery rather than jumping to anti-spin inputs.
PCL - IDLE.
CONTROLS - NEUTRAL, physically not just trimmed neutral.
ALTITUDE - CHECK.
RECOVER FROM UNUSUAL ATTITUDE once the stall breaks and the aircraft begins responding normally.
If the aircraft is not recovering as expected, it is common for the elevator to still be slightly aft of neutral; feed in forward stick only enough to find true neutral.
Do not start inventing anti-spin inputs early just because the motion feels dramatic.
If the aircraft is in an unrecoverable descent below 6000 feet AGL, eject.

items.text: Anti-spin recovery procedures are for a true steady-state spin, not for every out-of-control motion. The key is recognizing when neutral-controls recovery is no longer the right answer.

children.text: A steady-state erect spin is identified by 18+ units AOA, airspeed stabilized around 120-135 KIAS, and the turn needle fully deflected in the direction of spin.
At that point the spin has stabilized enough that anti-spin controls, not neutral controls, are required.
Apply full rudder opposite the turn-needle direction.
Immediately follow with smooth, positive forward stick to a position forward of neutral.
Keep ailerons neutral and hold the controls until rotation stops.
Then neutralize the controls, level the wings by horizon reference, make a smooth pullout, check oil pressure, and add power as required.
Progressive and aggravated spins are not handled by random experimentation; if the motion has not stabilized into a true steady-state picture, default back to OCF recovery logic.

Intentional inverted departures and inverted spins are prohibited. If an inverted-spin picture develops, the recovery inputs differ from erect-spin recovery and the aircraft requires post-flight scrutiny.
Power-on or inverted departures/spins place very high loads on the engine and propeller system and may produce low oil pressure or CHIP indications.
A spiral can look like a spin, but anti-spin inputs will not stop a spiral and may worsen it.
Do not hold full aft stick turn after turn waiting for the airplane to save you. Once the spin is clearly steady-state, transition to the proper anti-spin inputs.
Forward stick well beyond neutral can create oil-pressure issues and engine damage, and anti-spin logic should never replace proper phase recognition.

items.text: This event expects you to apply crosswind technique repeatedly, not just once. The student value is showing that the crosswind picture survives takeoff, touch-and-go, and full-stop landing without drifting back into late or sloppy corrections.

children.text: Use up to full aileron into the wind at the start of the takeoff roll, relax it as speed builds, and use rudder to stop weather-vaning.
Rotate firmly at flying speed to avoid skipping, then level the wings and let the aircraft crab into the wind once safely airborne.
On downwind and in the final turn, adjust bank and power for overshooting or undershooting winds and do not exceed 45 degrees of bank to make final.
Use the wing-low method on final: aileron into the wind to stop drift, rudder to align the nose with the runway, and extra power as required to offset cross-control drag.
During gusty conditions, add half the gust factor to final approach speed, up to 10 knots.
Do not level the wings in the flare. Land on the upwind main first with zero side motion.
On full stops, keep increasing aileron into the wind as the aircraft slows and the controls lose effectiveness.
On touch-and-goes, hold the crosswind controls on the deck, use positive rotation, then level the wings and allow the aircraft to crab into the wind after liftoff.
If you cannot prevent overshooting final without exceeding 45 degrees of bank, or if drift/crab is not under control before touchdown, wave off.
Skipping on takeoff, landing in a crab, and letting the upwind wing rise on rollout all come from losing the wind-correction picture as the aircraft slows or lifts off.
Do not aggressively yank the aircraft back to centerline after an off-center touchdown. Keep the wing under control first.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the boundaries straight: know what hydraulics powers, fly the spin entry cleanly, use neutral-controls OCF recovery until a true steady-state spin exists, and keep crosswind corrections alive all the way through touchdown.

events.summary: Hydraulic-system essentials, spin recognition, OCF versus anti-spin recovery, and repeated crosswind pattern application.

items.text: Start with purpose, then explain how normal hydraulic pressure is created and routed, then finish with what the emergency system does when the main system is gone. That sequence is much easier to brief than listing parts at random.

children.text: Purpose: provide hydraulic power for landing gear, flaps, speed brake, and nosewheel steering.
Normal-system flow: power package creates pressure, selector manifold routes it to the commanded service.
Emergency-system flow: accumulator pressure is saved for one-time emergency landing-gear and flap use.

items.text: The power package is the pressure-producing heart of the hydraulic system. It houses the reservoir, pump, and the components that regulate and protect system pressure.

children.text: The reservoir holds 5 quarts of hydraulic fluid, and the engine-driven pump maintains about 3000 +/- 120 PSI for the normal system.
A pressure reducer piston helps bring return pressure down, and the relief valve protects the system from overpressurization.
The pressure transmitter is what feeds the cockpit indication logic, and the filters are there to keep contamination from becoming a hydraulic problem.
The slide-valve assembly keeps the emergency system isolated during normal operations so the accumulator stays available for when you actually need it.
Think of 1800 PSI as the rough floor where the system still has enough pressure to do useful work, even though the normal target is much closer to 3000 PSI.

items.text: The selector manifold is the traffic cop. It takes pressure from the power package and sends it to the system you actually command from the cockpit.

children.text: Landing gear: the gear selector valve routes pressure to the main gear, nose gear, and inboard-door actuators. Three green lights mean down and locked; no lights mean up; a red light means transit or an associated gear-door condition.
Flaps: separate TO and LDG selector-valve paths let the flap actuator move the torque tube and flap system to the commanded setting.
Speed brake: hydraulic pressure extends it, and it auto-retracts with PCL to MAX, flap selection to LDG, or manual retract selection.
Nosewheel steering is hydraulically powered and gives about 12 degrees left or right of castor when engaged.
NWS is for ground steering only. If you need a sharper turn, disengage NWS before using differential braking so you are not fighting or damaging the steering system.
A speed brake that droops on the ramp is not automatically a malfunction; with pressure removed, the brake can settle because hydraulic pressure normally holds it up.

items.text: The emergency system is built around a helium-precharged accumulator that stores pressure for one-time emergency extension of the landing gear and flaps.

children.text: Pulling the emergency gear-extension handle releases accumulator pressure, isolates the main system, and ports pressure to the landing-gear and inboard-door actuators.
After emergency gear extension, the inboard doors remain extended. That is normal for the emergency configuration.
Emergency flap extension uses the same flap selector, but it is powered through the emergency path and the flaps cannot be retracted once extended.
A hydraulic fuse helps limit fluid loss into the emergency system if a leak develops.
An EHYD PX LO after emergency use is expected. EHYD PX LO together with HYDR FL LO is the combination that should make you think leak or fuse trouble instead of normal accumulator depletion.
If the emergency accumulator was discharged for maintenance, make sure the caution has cleared before flight so you do not launch with the backup already spent.

items.text: Most weak hydraulic briefs come from forgetting to tie indications back to what service you will actually lose next.

children.text: HYDR FL LO is a normal-system cue. EHYD PX LO is an emergency-system cue. Seeing both together means more than seeing either one alone.
Do not brief NWS as an isolated taxi feature; in this event it matters because a steering problem can become a takeoff, landing, or crosswind-control problem.
Be explicit that the emergency system is one-time use. Students often remember it exists but forget that you are spending stored pressure, not switching to a second normal system.

events.overview: This sortie is about using systems knowledge to make better recovery decisions. Be ready to brief the oil and propeller system at the event level, choose the correct airstart branch, and decide early whether the safer answer is a visual straight-in, a forced landing, or ejection.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4203 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full NATOPS-style walk-through. For this event, connect the oil and propeller system to the cockpit indications and decisions it drives.

children.text: The oil system is protecting engine bearings, the reduction gearbox, and the propeller interface unit, so a bad oil indication is never just a gauge problem until you prove it is.
The propeller is constant-speed and feathering, and normal RPM control depends on PMU and PIU control of oil pressure. If that logic degrades, thrust and drag change with it.
When PMU is OFF, increased oil pressure and volume can help counter an uncommanded feather, but the trade is higher pilot workload and tighter monitoring.

A momentary amber OIL PX caution while maneuvering may be nuisance, but a red OIL PX warning, persistent amber caution, oil-temperature problem, or visibly leaking oil should push you toward minimum necessary power and a PEL.
A CHIP warning means possible metal contamination in the engine or gearbox oil system. Treat it like damage that may get worse with power.
If FUEL PX also misbehaves, remember the external scavenge pump shares a shaft with the low-pressure fuel pump. That is why a fuel-pressure issue can reinforce the decision to continue the PEL.
If oil pressure looks normal while both red and amber oil indications are on, think SCU failure instead of real low oil pressure.
If OIL PX shows less than 5 PSI after a warning, the OIL TRX circuit breaker may be part of the picture, but do not let troubleshooting delay the landing decision.
PCL must be OFF to feather the propeller correctly for an airstart; that detail matters because the propeller and start logic are tied together.

items.text: All airstarts are starter-assisted and only buy you something if altitude, airspeed, and aircraft condition still support a recovery.

children.text: Primary envelope is 125-200 KIAS from sea level to 15,000 feet and 135-200 KIAS from 15,001-20,000 feet. Starts are only demonstrated up to 20,000 feet MSL.
Plan on more than 1200 feet of altitude loss and about 40 seconds to useful power for a normal attempt.
Use PMU NORM unless the PMU FAIL warning is illuminated. If PMU is bad, the PMU OFF airstart becomes a manual fuel-metering problem.
PCL OFF first, then confirm the starter, ignition, boost pump, firewall shutoff, and bleed-air setup before you introduce fuel.
For PMU NORM or immediate airstarts, move the PCL to IDLE above 13% N1 and do not advance above IDLE until N1 stabilizes at about 67%.
For a PMU OFF airstart, starter stays in MANUAL and the critical pilot task is smooth PCL movement while watching fuel flow, ITT, and N1.
If N1 does not rise within 5 seconds, or ITT does not rise within 10 seconds after fuel flow, stop the attempt and go back to OFF.
If the start fails, the next answer is forced landing or ejection, not endless troubleshooting.
Below 2000 feet AGL, do not let the hope of a successful airstart delay the ejection decision.

items.text: Ejection is the correct answer once continued flight is no longer survivable; it is not the backup plan after every other option has already failed.

children.text: Controlled ejection assumes the aircraft is still flyable long enough to optimize conditions. Recommended minimum is 2000 feet AGL and roughly 125-180 KIAS.
Uncontrolled ejection means the aircraft is no longer controllable. Recommended minimum is 6000 feet AGL, but if the aircraft is truly unrecoverable you eject immediately.
Make the decision early. The seat can work at very low altitude, but pilot delay, attitude, sink rate, and airspeed are what destroy margins.
If time permits: notify the other crewmember, make a distress call, set 7700, stow loose gear, get visor down, tighten mask and helmet, check leg garters and harness, and set ADU as required.
Release the emergency oxygen hose from the elastic sidewall strap before ejecting or you may lose the emergency oxygen supply.
PCL goes OFF, turn toward an uninhabited area if able, then assume the proper position before pulling.
Use the ORM 3-2-1 mindset during a forced-landing profile: below 2000 feet AGL you should only keep descending if you are on profile, runway in sight, and in a position to land.
If those criteria are not met by the bottom of the profile, the real-world answer may be ejection. In training, that same decision point becomes a waveoff.
If ejecting over mountainous terrain above 8000 feet MSL, be ready to use the MOR handle for manual seat separation and chute deployment.

items.text: A visual straight-in is the recovery option when an overhead or break is not practical and you still have enough runway picture to stabilize early.

children.text: Establish ATC contact early and position 3-5 NM from the runway on extended centerline, extended base, or a 45-degree intercept that still gives you time to stabilize.
Slow below 150 KIAS for configuration, get the gear down, and finish the Before Landing Checklist no later than the base-to-final setup or 3-5 NM final.
Confirm the local reporting and pattern flow from the current SOP or day-of brief instead of memorizing one field's named checkpoints.
Build a stabilized glideslope of roughly 400-600 feet per NM and fly the normal 110/105/100 KIAS picture for the selected flap setting.
Be wings level with adequate straightaway by about 200 feet AGL, with the runway centerline already under control instead of still being chased.
Report gear down, verify landing clearance, and do not let late radio work distract from the landing picture.
If the straight-in is no longer stable, do not force it. In training that means waveoff; in an emergency it may mean forced landing or ejection depending on what margin is left.
Late configuration, low energy, or trying to salvage a drifting final is what turns a planned straight-in into a bad recovery problem.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the decision tree straight: know what the oil and propeller indications mean, know which airstart branch you are in, and do not let straight-in or ejection criteria become last-second calls.

events.summary: Oil/propeller system big picture, airstart branch selection, and the ejection-versus-straight-in decisions that follow a bad engine day.

systemsBrief.headline: Systems brief

items.text: Start with purpose, then walk the flow path, then explain what cockpit indication changes the operational answer. That order keeps the brief from turning into disconnected component trivia.

children.text: Purpose: lubricate, cool, and protect the engine, gearbox, and propeller-control components.
Flow: where oil comes from, where it goes under pressure, how it is scavenged and cooled, and how it returns.
Indications and consequences: what OIL PX, oil temperature, CHIP, NP, or feathering behavior should make you say next.

items.text: The oil system is a self-contained, dry-sump, pressurized system with pressure, scavenge, cooling, and breather subsystems. Tank capacity is 18.5 quarts.

children.text: The engine-driven oil pump is a single-stage, gear-driven pump inside the tank and is driven by the accessory gearbox.
Normal flight uses the lower pickup; inverted flight uses the upper pickup so oil supply continues in changing attitudes.
Pressurized oil is delivered to the AGB bearings, gas-generator bearings, power-turbine bearings, RGB, and PIU.
Internal and external scavenge pumps return used oil from bearings, turbines, gearbox, and propeller components.
Oil passes through the cooler before returning to the tank. The oil cooler uses outside air from the inlet below the starter-generator inlet.
The breather system vents pressure and oil vapor overboard while spinning residual oil back toward the tank.
Normal oil-pressure thinking: 15-40 PSI at idle is caution range, less than 15 PSI at idle is warning, and with PCL above idle anything under 40 PSI is a warning.
Normal in-flight oil-temperature range is 10-105°C. Ground operations can transiently use 106-110°C if torque is below 20 percent.
If both red and amber oil indications are on with normal pressure, think SCU failure. If FUEL PX joins the problem, remember the shared shaft with the external scavenge pump.

items.text: The propeller is a 97-inch, four-bladed, constant-speed, variable-pitch, non-reversing, feathering propeller. Normal speed is 2000 RPM or 100% NP.

children.text: The reduction gearbox takes engine RPM down to usable propeller RPM and drives the propeller, PIU, and torque-probe system.
The PIU uses engine oil and PMU commands to change blade pitch and hold 100% NP.
Increasing oil pressure drives the piston forward and moves the blades toward fine pitch; loss of oil pressure lets the counterweights and feathering spring drive the blades toward feather.
Normal feathering is commanded with PCL to CUTOFF and PMU in NORM, which drains prop-servo oil pressure.
PCL must be OFF to feather correctly during airstarts. If the PROP SYS circuit breaker is out, feathering may be delayed or incomplete.
With PMU OFF, counterweights dump oil and spring force drives the prop toward coarse pitch, so brief the higher workload and possible transient NP overspeed.
Avoid sustained ground operation between 62-80% NP because of resonance risk.
Propeller overspeed limit is 110% NP.
If rapid RPM changes trigger a PMU sensor-rate red X, cycling the PMU can clear it only if the issue is not a true sensor failure.

events.overview: This sortie is about managing an electrical or avionics problem without letting it turn into a navigation or communication-control problem. Be ready to explain the electrical system at the brief level, recognize which avionics failures are survivable with backups, and fly the lost-comms recovery plan in a transferable way.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4204 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full bus-by-bus NATOPS walk-through. For this event, know what still has power, what is automatically shed, and what that means for your next decision.

children.text: Normal power comes from the 28 VDC starter-generator, with the main battery, auxiliary battery, and hot battery bus preserving different pieces of capability when generation is lost.

If the generator fails, only air conditioning is automatically shed at first. A bus-tie problem or deeper electrical failure is what starts changing which cockpit displays, radios, and avionics stay alive.
If the bus tie opens, the battery side and generator side stop supporting each other, so know which buses and avionics you lose before you start chasing secondary failures.
A GEN warning does not mean the whole jet is dark immediately. Think about battery endurance, what the auxiliary battery is protecting, and what the hot battery bus still carries.
A BUS TIE caution can explain why one side of the cockpit picture is still healthy while another is degrading.
Electrical smoke or fumes is a control-and-survival problem first. If aircraft control is jeopardized, CFS or ejection is already on the table.
The generator needs at least 25 volts to charge the batteries.
Do not connect external power with battery voltage below 22 volts.
Hot battery bus circuit breakers are not accessible in flight, so do not brief them like normal reset options.

items.text: Most avionics malfunctions are really cross-check and backup-instrument problems before they become checklist problems.

children.text: If displays disagree or go blank, verify what the other cockpit sees and transition early to the BFI or other surviving instruments instead of waiting for the picture to get worse.

IAC, IRS, ADC, EDM, and UFCP failures all change a different part of the picture, so brief what you lose, what backup instrument replaces it, and whether the right answer is to keep troubleshooting or land as soon as practical.
Audio, transponder, ADS-B, and AOA failures are usually survivable, but they change how visible or communicative you are to ATC and how much primary information you can trust.
Do not select REPEAT in the cockpit with working MFDs when the other side has an IAC failure or erratic displays.
If the ADC fails, expect loss of primary airspeed, altitude, and VSI along with secondary items like gear aural warning and transponder Mode C, so the BFI becomes the reference.
If the EDM fails, you may lose the ability to trust displayed fuel, hydraulic, electrical, and pressurization monitoring even though caution messages can still appear.
Check the relevant circuit breaker if it is available, but do not burn the whole event cycling breakers on hot or inaccessible buses.
If the avionics picture does not recover cleanly, the default answer is land as soon as practical.

items.text: Lost communications is a predictability problem first: keep VMC if able, stay separated, and make it easy for ATC and other aircraft to understand what you are doing.

children.text: Squawk 7600, make all calls in the blind, and if you can receive but not transmit use IDENT to acknowledge instructions.
Try every practical path back into the radios: UHF, VHF, backup VHF, guard, and manual frequency entry.
Do not let a NORDO situation drift into poor geometry or surprise traffic conflicts just because you are heads-down troubleshooting.
If you recover enough radio capability to coordinate, do it early. If not, keep flying the published lost-comms plan instead of improvising a new one.
If you are receive-only, use the information you can still hear to stay predictable and acknowledge with IDENT when appropriate.

items.text: Know the current home-field and local-area lost-comms recovery plan, but study it as a process rather than a list of Corpus-specific named points.

children.text: If you are already on a local arrival or recovery, continue with the published NORDO reentry from the current SOP instead of inventing a shortcut.
Expect to make blind calls, watch for ALDIS or light-gun signals, and be ready to wave off and try the pattern again if you do not have a clear landing signal.
Brief the local named entry points, route names, and runway-flow specifics from the day-of SOP; do not rely on yesterday's memory.
Your job is to arrive where the controlling agency expects you, at the expected altitude and speed, with a predictable plan for another pattern if clearance never becomes obvious.
If the runway picture, signal, or traffic situation is not clear, wave off and re-fly the plan instead of forcing the landing.

studyNotes.summary: Keep the priorities straight: know what still has power, cross-check with backups early, communicate blind and squawk 7600, then execute the current lost-comms plan instead of guessing.

events.summary: Electrical-system big picture, avionics-failure triage, and generalized lost-comms recovery planning.

systemsBrief.headline: Systems brief

items.text: Lead with power sources, then explain how the buses distribute that power, then finish with what stays alive when the system starts shedding or separating.

children.text: Power source: starter-generator, main battery, auxiliary battery, and external power.
Distribution: battery bus, generator bus, avionics buses, auxiliary battery bus, and hot battery bus.
Failure logic: bus-tie behavior, automatic shedding, and which systems remain powered long enough to matter.

items.text: Normal electrical power is 28 VDC from a 300-amp starter-generator. The generator becomes the primary source once the engine reaches about 50% N1.

children.text: The main battery is a 24 VDC, 42-amp-hour battery in the nose and is the primary backup if generation is lost.
The auxiliary battery is a 24 VDC, 5-amp-hour battery that protects an isolated emergency bus carrying items such as the BFI, backup VHF, and fire-warning logic.
External power is 28 VDC for ground use and requires BAT ON; do not connect it if battery voltage is below 22 volts.
The generator needs to supply at least 25 volts to charge the batteries.
If the generator fails, only air conditioning is automatically shed immediately.

items.text: The split-bus architecture lets the aircraft isolate loads while still giving both cockpits a useful picture under normal conditions.

children.text: Battery bus carries items such as ICS, trim, TAD, GPS, and engine instruments.
Generator bus carries items such as EICAS, EFIS, PMU, and radio control.
Avionics Bus #1 and #2 split major avionics loads between the front and aft sides of the airplane.
The auxiliary battery bus is isolated from the primary system and protects emergency-use items.
The hot battery bus stays powered directly from the main battery even with BAT OFF and supports items like the RAM air valve, ELT, FDR, OBOGS, and emergency flaps.
Hot battery bus circuit breakers are not accessible in flight.

items.text: The bus tie normally connects the battery and generator sides so the aircraft can share power and recharge correctly.

children.text: If the bus tie opens or fails, the battery side only powers the battery bus and Avionics Bus #1, while the generator side only powers the generator bus and Avionics Bus #2.
That split is why one display set or radio stack can remain alive while another part of the cockpit degrades.
Load shedding and clean prioritization matter after a bus-tie failure because you may not get the full airplane back.
In smoke-and-fume or electrical-fire situations, OBOGS setup comes first and the next question is whether aircraft control is still assured.
If the source of smoke is clearly identified and accessible, you can secure it or pull the appropriate circuit breaker, but inaccessible hot-bus items remove that option.

events.overview: This sortie is about recognizing an abnormal situation early enough to stop, recover, or re-enter cleanly before it stacks into something worse. Be ready to brief the OBOGS and pressurization system at the event level, abort decisively on the ground, recover methodically when lost, and know when damaged-aircraft logic or a discontinued entry protects you from creating a second emergency.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4301 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the dense OBOGS and pressurization walk-through. For this event, know what the system is doing for you, what the cockpit warnings really mean, and when you must treat it like a survival problem instead of a nuisance indication.

children.text: OBOGS uses conditioned bleed air and a molecular-sieve concentrator to provide each pilot an essentially unlimited oxygen source, while emergency seat oxygen covers the true failure case.
Pressurization holds cockpit altitude around 8000 feet until the differential-pressure limit is reached, then lets cockpit altitude rise as the aircraft climbs.
Dump and RAM/DUMP remove pressurization on purpose, so know whether the cockpit is unpressurized because you selected it or because the system is failing.
An OBOGS FAIL warning can come from low bleed-air pressure, low oxygen concentration, or internal system trouble; if the engine is gone or electrical power is gone, OBOGS is gone too.
A loose mask or mask-off condition can reduce oxygen available to both cockpits and create a misleading OBOGS FAIL.
CKPT ALT, CKPT PX, and DUCT TEMP tell you whether the problem is cockpit pressure, differential pressure, or hot bleed air instead of oxygen generation alone.
If smoke, fumes, or loss of oxygen jeopardizes aircraft control, emergency oxygen, CFS, or ejection may already be the safer answer.
After power loss or system deactivation, OBOGS has a 4-minute warm-up period before concentration warnings are reliable again.
White zeolite dust from a failed concentrator is a real warning sign; avoid inhaling it, but remember oxygen concentration may still be adequate.

items.text: An abort is the answer for any abnormal or unsafe condition before max abort speed. Decide early, say it clearly, and stop the aircraft before the problem grows teeth.

children.text: Prior to max abort speed, the immediate actions are PCL IDLE and BRAKES AS REQUIRED with smooth, single-application braking.
Maintain directional control with rudder and nosewheel steering, and make the ICS abort call only after the aircraft is under control.
If you can taxi clear, do it. If not, transition to emergency shutdown and ground egress logic as required.
Max abort speed is the earlier of 1500 feet or 60 KIAS unless performance planning gives you a lower limit.
Above 80 KIAS, braking gets less effective because lift is still unloading the wheels.
Do not brake before full weight is on wheels, and if the aircraft starts to get away laterally, release and reapply instead of staying locked on the brakes.
After maximum-effort braking, do not set the parking brake and do not taxi into a congested area until you are confident the brakes have cooled.
Most tire blowouts happen early, especially before spin-up or below about 40 KIAS, so do not hold brake pressure mindlessly at the bottom end.

items.text: When you are lost, the fix is disciplined process, not random maneuvering. Fly the aircraft, stay VFR if at all possible, and work the Five Cs early.

children.text: CONFESS early and ask for help.
CLIMB if conditions permit to improve radio range and visibility.
CONSERVE by flying maximum-endurance AOA, about 8.8 units or 125 ± 8 KIAS, in straight-and-level flight.
COMMUNICATE with the instructor aircraft, ODO/FDO, approach, or Guard, and pass fuel, souls, position, and intentions.
COMPLY with vectors or recovery guidance once help is established.
Use FMS nearest, known landmarks, and a methodical scan to rebuild the picture instead of wandering around hoping something looks familiar.
If you still cannot reorient, pick a suitable airfield, orbit safely to evaluate wind and obstacles, and land full stop rather than running the fuel state down.
Do not descend below your safe altitude floor just to try to regain VMC or recognition.

items.text: A discontinued entry is the escape maneuver when pattern entry geometry, traffic separation, or radio coordination is no longer safe enough to continue inbound.

children.text: Execute it when the controlling agency directs it, when traffic separation is not confirmed by the published decision gate, when runway alignment is wrong, or when the interval picture is no longer trustworthy.
Turn away from the inbound runway heading early enough to deconflict, stay at the published entry altitude until clear, and do not overfly the field unless the local procedure explicitly requires it.
Reenter using the current published recovery point and pattern plan from the day-of SOP instead of carrying yesterday's named-route memory into a busy pattern.
If the radio picture is weak or you are NORDO, visual deconfliction and predictability matter even more. When in doubt, discontinue and try again.
The aircraft not yet established in the pattern carries the larger deconfliction burden.

items.text: Airborne-damaged aircraft handling starts with a simple question: is the aircraft controllable? If not, eject. If yes, buy time, evaluate, and recover with a plan.

children.text: Maintain aircraft control, terminate the maneuver, and analyze the situation before you start moving switches.
Use the crew, another aircraft, or the controlling agency to help assess damage extent if the picture is uncertain.
If the prop arc or engine is involved, or engine indications are abnormal, default toward PEL logic.
If the aircraft is controllable and the damage picture is unclear, climb to at least 6500 feet AGL if practical and run a controllability check.
Slow gradually toward landing configuration, but never below 90 KIAS or stick shaker, whichever is higher.
If flap damage is suspected, do not reposition the flaps just to see what happens.
Avoid abrupt control inputs with structural damage.
Do not lower gear or flaps until you understand whether the aircraft can tolerate the configuration change.
If the aircraft becomes uncontrollable at any point, eject.

studyNotes.summary: Recognize the abnormal early, then choose the right recovery path: survive the OBOGS problem, abort decisively, recover methodically when lost, and do not let entry or damage confusion create a second emergency.

events.summary: OBOGS and pressurization fundamentals, decisive abort logic, and airborne recovery judgment when the normal plan falls apart.

systemsBrief.headline: Systems brief

items.text: Lead with oxygen generation, then explain regulation and backup oxygen, then move to pressurization control and cockpit indications. That order matches how students are usually walked through the brief.

children.text: OBOGS: bleed-air source, concentrator, plenum, regulators, and emergency backup.
Pressurization: control valve, dump logic, delta-P limit, and cockpit-altitude indications.
Finish with the warnings and cautions that change the operational answer.

items.text: OBOGS uses conditioned engine bleed air, a heat exchanger, water separator, and a molecular-sieve concentrator to generate breathable oxygen for both cockpits.

children.text: The plenum downstream of the concentrator carries a short reserve while the system stabilizes or if concentration dips.
Each regulator has a supply lever, concentration lever, pressure lever, BIT button, and flow indicator.
MAX concentration in one cockpit drives MAX concentration to both cockpits.
BIT is available manually or during power-up, and the FAIL annunciator behavior is part of the normal check.
The system has a 4-minute warm-up period after activation or power interruption before oxygen-concentration warnings are fully reliable.
Emergency oxygen is independent of OBOGS and is activated from the ejection seat.

items.text: Pressurization uses engine bleed air and valve logic to hold cockpit altitude near 8000 feet until the differential-pressure limit of about 3.6 ± 0.2 PSI is reached.

children.text: The control valve, control-valve regulator, dump solenoid, safety valve, and delta-P regulator are the heart of the system.
The pressurization switch selects NORM, DUMP, or RAM/DUMP, with RAM/DUMP also opening the fresh-air path and closing defog.
At about 18,069 feet pressure altitude the system has reached its delta-P limit, so cockpit altitude starts rising from there.
CKPT ALT, CKPT PX, and DUCT TEMP are the key cockpit indications for the pressurization side.
If cockpit pressure readings differ materially from 3.6 ± 0.2 PSI above the crossover altitude, maintenance needs to hear about it.
Air conditioning does not degrade engine or aircraft performance, so do not invent a performance penalty that is not there.

events.overview: This sortie shifts into fuel-system decision making and disciplined full-stop landing execution. Be ready to explain how fuel is stored, balanced, and delivered, then apply that knowledge to heavy-weight landings and to the critical-action EPs that can suddenly turn a normal recovery into a full-stop or emergency problem.

notes: Adjust specifics to match the assigned profile, weather, and local procedures.
Because the blocks are shared, one edit updates every event that references the same procedure or comm call.
scriptTemplate.title: FAM4302 Script

studyNotes.headline: Discussion items

items.text: Use the Systems brief tool for the full tank, probe, and pump walk-through. For this event, know what fuel-system cues matter in flight and which ones change whether you keep maneuvering, knock off aerobatics, or start working an abnormal recovery.

children.text: The collector tank is what keeps the engine fed in unusual attitudes, and the flip-flop valve is what gives you limited inverted fuel instead of a magic unlimited supply.
Automatic fuel balancing should quietly handle normal imbalances. When it does not, your job is to recognize whether you have a simple imbalance, a probe problem, or a real feed issue.
Minimum aerobatic fuel is 150 pounds per side, and max imbalance is 50 pounds. Those are event-useful numbers because they change what you can safely keep doing.
FUEL PX means motive-flow pressure is low and should drive an immediate cross-check of boost-pump status, fuel flow, and engine behavior.
FP FAIL means the quantity-probe logic has failed and automatic balancing is gone, but the independent L/R FUEL LO lights are still trustworthy.
If boost-pump operation or low-pressure warnings show up during inverted flight or aerobatics, stop the maneuvering and treat it as a maintenance-significant fuel-system cue.
Do not manually balance fuel with FP FAIL active because the quantity picture may be wrong and you can make the imbalance worse.
Fuel flow at or above 800 PPH is not a normal number to ignore; it can be the first sign of a malfunction that becomes an engine problem.
Treat repeated auto-balance resets as a clue that the system is not really healthy, not just as a way to keep the caution light quiet.

items.text: A full-stop landing is about disciplined touchdown and rollout, not just arriving over the runway. In this event, show that you can land on the mains, keep the aircraft straight, and manage aerodynamic braking all the way to taxi speed.

children.text: Arrive with the Before Landing Checklist complete, gear down, the correct flap setting, and an on-speed final picture for the selected configuration.
Clear final, confirm winds and runway status early, and have the rollout plan in mind before the flare starts.
If crosswind is present, plan to keep those corrections alive through touchdown and rollout instead of relaxing them once the mains touch.
At about 5-10 feet AGL, smoothly retard the PCL to IDLE once landing is assured and transition to a normal flared landing.
Touch down on the main gear in a controlled nose-high attitude, then keep back-stick in long enough to use aerodynamic braking before lowering the nose wheel.
Use rudder for directional control during the early rollout and bring brakes in smoothly below 80 KIAS instead of stabbing at them while the aircraft is still light.
If the landing picture is no longer stable, if directional control is deteriorating, or if the runway-remaining picture is becoming unsafe, wave off early instead of trying to salvage it.
Do not rush into NWS. Let the aircraft decelerate into a true taxi-speed regime before you start asking the steering system to help.
A heavy touchdown, a nosewheel touchdown above 80 KIAS, or an aggressive brake application can turn a routine full stop into a blown-tire or hard-landing problem quickly.

items.text: Heavy-weight landings are not a separate technique so much as a tighter version of the normal landing. The aircraft is less forgiving, the sink rate builds faster, and the rollout margin shrinks if you arrive slow, flat, or long.

children.text: When fuel state is above about 700-800 pounds, add roughly 3-5 KIAS in the approach turn as briefed and guard against letting the aircraft get slow.
Cross-check the amber donut with airspeed instead of flying one cue in isolation. Heavy aircraft can still get behind the power curve quickly.
Make sure runway length, braking plan, and crosswind picture are good enough before you commit to the landing.
Expect slower pitch and power response, a more deliberate flare, and a longer ground roll.
Touch down on-speed and on aimpoint. Heavy-weight landings become ugly when students float, then force the aircraft on late.
Bring braking in smoothly after the nosewheel is firmly on deck and expect more heat and less forgiveness than a lighter aircraft gives you.
Brake fade, hot brakes, and blown tires become more believable after a heavy landing, especially if you ride the brakes or arrive fast.
Do not let the heavier feel trick you into flying below on-speed AOA to pin the airplane on early.
Crosswind demands increase with weight because the airplane is slower to respond, so stay ahead of the control inputs rather than reacting late.

items.text: Treat this as a cumulative EP review where the instructor may move quickly from recognition to immediate action to the follow-on decision. Use the dedicated EP and N/W/C references as the verbatim lane, and use this section to keep the decision tree organized.

children.text: Be ready for the ground and departure set: Fire on the Ground, Emergency Engine Shutdown on the Ground, Emergency Ground Egress, Abort Takeoff, Aircraft Departs Prepared Surface, and Engine Failure Immediately After Takeoff.
Be ready for the airborne engine set: Engine Failure During Flight, Immediate Air-Start, PMU NORM Air-Start, PMU OFF Air-Start, and Uncommanded Power Changes/LOP.
Know the branch points that turn an EP into a PEL, forced landing, or ejection problem. That is usually where the grading value is, not just whether you can chant the memory items.
Lead with the recognition cue, then the critical action, then the follow-on landing or eject logic.
Do not separate the EP from its N/W/Cs. The warning or caution is often the part that changes the safe answer.
If an EP briefing stalls out because you cannot explain the next safe recovery option, go back and rebuild the decision chain instead of memorizing one more isolated step.

studyNotes.summary: Know the fuel cues that matter, land the aircraft all the way to taxi speed, and keep the critical-action EP decision tree organized enough that you do not hesitate when the sortie changes pace.

events.summary: Fuel-system study, full-stop landing execution, heavy-weight landing traps, and critical-action EP review.

items.text: Start with tank layout and usable fuel, then explain how the quantity and balance logic works, then walk the engine feed path. That order sounds like a brief instead of a scavenger hunt through component names.

children.text: Purpose: store fuel, indicate usable quantity accurately, balance the wings automatically, and keep the engine fed in normal and unusual attitudes.
Big picture: wing tanks feed the collector, the collector feeds the engine, and the system has both motive-flow and electrically assisted backup paths.
Operational payoff: once you understand where the fuel is, how it moves, and what the cautions mean, FUEL PX, BOOST PUMP, FUEL BAL, and FP FAIL are much easier to interpret.

items.text: The aircraft has three fuel tanks: left wing, right wing, and a collector tank. That layout is the foundation for the whole brief.

children.text: Usable fuel is 1100 pounds with single-point refueling and 1200 pounds with over-wing refueling. The collector tank holds about 40 pounds, with the remainder split across the wing tanks.
Single-point refueling is the normal method because it refuels all tanks together. Over-wing refueling adds about 100 pounds total and fills the tanks by gravity.
Fuel approved for use includes the normal JP-series and Jet A family fuels, but the student briefing value is usually in the tank layout and usable-fuel numbers, not in reciting every fuel type.

items.text: The fuel-quantity and balancing logic is what keeps a simple tank layout from becoming a bad asymmetry problem.

children.text: There are seven quantity probes total: three in each wing and one in the collector. The probe system feeds the EICAS quantity bars and the balancing logic.

Automatic balancing starts if the system sees more than about 20 pounds of imbalance for more than 30 seconds. It closes the transfer valve to the light tank so the heavy tank keeps feeding until the difference comes back down.
If imbalance stays above about 30 pounds for two minutes, FUEL BAL illuminates. Manual reset buys another timer cycle, but it should also make you ask why the system is not self-correcting.
Max imbalance is 50 pounds, and aerobatics are prohibited below 150 pounds per side.
L/R FUEL LO comes from independent optical sensors at less than about 110 pounds per wing, which is why it still matters even if FP FAIL has taken out the probe-based logic.
M FUEL BAL means manual balancing is selected. That may be a deliberate pilot action, but it should never become a substitute for understanding why the automatic system gave up.

items.text: The engine-feed path is the part students most often memorize poorly, so walk it in order and keep the backup paths straight.

children.text: Wing tanks feed transfer jet pumps, which move fuel into the collector tank. From the collector, the flip-flop valve selects the pickup point so the engine can keep receiving fuel in unusual attitudes, including about 60 seconds of inverted flight.

From there, fuel reaches the primary jet pump in normal operations or the electric boost pump when backup or startup help is needed, then goes through the manifold valve, fuel filter, engine low-pressure pump, high-pressure pump, FMU, flow divider, and the 14 fuel nozzles.

The electric boost pump comes on for startup, low-pressure backup, and other commanded conditions. The high-pressure pump can suction-feed, but that is a limited mode, not the preferred steady-state answer.

items.text: The best fuel-system briefs end by tying the cockpit cautions back to what is probably failing and what the pilot should do next.

children.text: FUEL PX means motive-flow pressure is low. BOOST PUMP can be a commanded response to that low-pressure condition, to startup, or to manual selection.
FP FAIL means the probe system failed and automatic balancing is disabled. FUEL BAL means the system tried to correct an imbalance and could not get it back under control in the allotted time.
Do not manually balance with FP FAIL active, and do not shrug off fuel flow above 799 PPH or abnormal boost-pump behavior in aerobatics as just a nuisance indication.
