studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: The approach maneuver simulates a low-altitude instrument approach from over a NAVAID while forcing clean scan, timing, descent control, BAC transition, and missed-approach discipline.

children.text: Start at 200 KIAS in straight-and-level flight on a cardinal heading.
Slow toward 150 KIAS with about 15% torque; anticipate left rudder and trim right rudder plus up elevator as the aircraft decelerates.
Approaching 150 KIAS, add power to about 33% to maintain level flight and re-trim.
Turn right standard rate, not to exceed 30 degrees AOB, for 90 degrees of heading change while maintaining altitude and using the one-third rollout rule.
After the 90-degree turn, start the clock for two minutes, set about 15% torque, and descend 1000 feet at 150 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
About 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 33% and level at 150 KIAS.
At the end of two minutes, begin a left standard-rate turn for 210 degrees; anticipate a small need for power and back-stick pressure to hold level flight at 150 KIAS.
After the 210-degree turn, slow down first, then go down: reduce power to about 15% and maintain altitude to expedite deceleration.
Below 150 KIAS, lower the gear, set flaps to T/O, and execute the Before Landing Checklist.
At 120 KIAS, lower the nose and descend 1000 feet; about 100 feet before level-off, add power to about 42% to maintain 120 KIAS.
Stabilize on altitude and heading, reset the clock, set about 15% torque again, and descend another 1000 feet at 120 KIAS and about 1000 FPM.
At the end of the second two-minute timing segment, execute the missed approach: max power, right rudder, and 10 to 15 degrees nose high.
Check VSI and altimeter, call two positive rates and raise the gear; above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps.
Report gear and flaps up before 150 KIAS, then set 8 to 10 degrees nose high and accelerate toward 180 KIAS while climbing 2000 feet.
Start the 200 KIAS cruise transition about 200 feet before level-off.
The maneuver is complete at 200 KIAS, on the heading used after the 210-degree turn, and 1000 feet below the original starting altitude.

The event's special navigation requirement is to proceed direct to homefield using an available NAVAID when directed; brief the navigation method as part of the approach setup, not as a separate discussion item.
Common errors are late power changes, poor trim through BAC, chasing rate with pitch instead of power, and missing gear/flap cleanup during the missed approach.

items.text: IFR unusual-attitude recovery is an instrument scan and verification problem: recognize the bad attitude, confirm it against backup/performance instruments, and recover without creating a worse energy state.

children.text: An unusual attitude is any unexpected or inadvertent attitude encountered during normal instrument flight.
To avoid the situation in IMC, roll should normally be limited to 30 degrees AOB, nose low to 10 degrees, and nose high to 15 degrees.
Common causes include slow scan, spatial disorientation, fixation on a subtask, and transition from VFR to IFR.
Recognize with attitude indicator and performance cues, then confirm actual attitude with the BFI and performance instruments before recovering.
Relax back-stick pressure while maintaining positive G so the nose can fall toward the horizon.
Roll toward, but not past, 90 degrees of bank; use only as much bank as needed.
If climbing, use power as required to keep airspeed above stall.
As the miniature aircraft approaches the horizon, adjust bank toward wings level; if airspeed is below 100 KIAS, the nose may continue below the horizon until safe flying speed is restored.
Roll wings level first.
Start the pull only after the wings are level.
Approaching 200 KIAS or greater, reduce power and use speed brake if required to stay below maximum allowable airspeed.
Recovery is complete when the aircraft is back in the desired attitude for normal instrument flight.
Common nose-high errors are pushing negative G, not rolling enough toward 90 degrees when needed, and failing to add power.
Common nose-low errors are pulling before wings level and forgetting to reset power or speed brake after recovery.

items.text: In I2103, IMC emergency thinking is tied directly to unusual attitudes and avionics failures: stabilize first, then troubleshoot.

children.text: Use the NATOPS emergency priorities: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation and take proper action, then land as soon as conditions permit.
Critical action memory items are completed immediately when required; time permitting, back them up with the checklist.
In IMC, protect altitude, attitude, terrain clearance, and ATC coordination before local convenience or troubleshooting flow.

For inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or an IMC abort, maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit.
Squawk and declare as required, tell ATC your intentions, and avoid a heads-down troubleshooting posture until the aircraft is stable.
If the emergency is an avionics failure, transition to the BFI or remaining reliable instruments before touching repeat switches or circuit breakers.

items.text: Dual IAC failure is an avionics-failure event that can remove the normal flight-display picture; the first answer is to fly the aircraft from backup references before troubleshooting.

children.text: Dual IAC failure results in loss of HUD, UFCP, and MFD displays in both cockpits.
A single IAC failure may not show an IAC failure message, but may cause MFD loss in one or both cockpits, erratic MFD behavior, HUD or UFCP malfunction, or synchronization errors.
Synchronization errors can show up as mismatched heading, altitude, or airspeed bugs between cockpits, QNH DISAGREE on the FMS, or incorrect REPEAT-mode behavior.
If synchronization errors or erratic indications are detected on the ground, takeoff is not recommended.
If synchronization errors exist without MFD loss, do not select REPEAT in either cockpit.
Do not select REPEAT from a cockpit with working MFDs during suspected crosstalk or synchronization failure; it may lead to loss of all MFD information in both cockpits.
Reference the BFI as required.
Set the NORM/REPEAT switch to NORM in both cockpits.
Check IAC1 and IAC2 circuit breakers on the left and right front console and reset if open.
If IAC/MFD failures or erratic displays persist, pull the failed IAC circuit breaker or breakers, then reset after 5 seconds.
If failures, erratic displays, or synchronization errors persist, land as soon as practical.

items.text: The BFI is the backup attitude and performance reference that keeps the aircraft flyable after PFD, ADC, IRU, or IAC failures.

children.text: The BFI is in the upper right side of the instrument panel in both cockpits.
It provides attitude, altitude, airspeed, heading, and vertical velocity.
It is normally powered by the battery bus; with a battery-bus failure, the auxiliary battery can power it through the AUX BAT switch.
The front cockpit circuit breaker is STBY INST; rear cockpit BFI power is through AFT STBY on the front-cockpit panel.
The adjustment knob changes baro; pushing it sets STD 29.92.
The M push-button enters or exits menu mode.
Useful menu items include FAST ERECT, SET BRIGHTNESS, FAST ALIGN, and SET HEADING when no external heading data is available.
FAST ERECT requires straight-and-level, non-accelerated flight.
If the PFD is partly or fully lost, reference the BFI, smoothly level the wings with coordinated rudder and aileron, and set the nose to straight-and-level attitude.
Once the aircraft is stabilized, complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure.
The common error is rushing into an emergency procedure before the aircraft is stabilized in straight-and-level BFI flight.
ATT FAIL removes pitch ladder, roll pointer, and slip/skid while leaving roll scale and aircraft symbol on a cyan background.
Processor errors may show as a red X or a black screen with instructions.

studyNotes.summary: Fly the approach maneuver precisely, then show that unusual attitudes, IMC emergencies, IAC failures, and BFI-only flight all start with the same control-first instrument discipline.

events.overview: I2201 turns the HSI into a usable position picture. The event standard is to know where the station, aircraft, bearing pointer, and CDI are telling you to go, then use that picture to go direct, track, identify station passage, and intercept radials without chasing the display.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: HSI orientation starts with a mental model: the NAVAID is at the center of the compass card, and the aircraft is on the tail of the bearing pointer.

children.text: The compass rose rotates with aircraft heading; the aircraft symbol stays fixed at the top of the display.
Bearing pointer #1 is the green single-line pointer and bearing pointer #2 is the cyan double-line pointer; the head points toward the selected source and the tail shows the radial you are on.

The CDI course arrow shows the selected VOR course or FMS track, the deviation bar shows lateral displacement, and the TO/FROM arrow tells whether that selected course is taking you to or from the station.
Unless you are tracking directly to or from the NAVAID, forward motion makes heads fall and tails rise.
Tie every answer back to present position: station in the center, aircraft on the tail, desired course in the CDI, and turn direction from the relationship between them.
The event may remove CDI help and require bearing-pointer/heading-bug work, so brief the bearing-pointer logic instead of memorizing one display setup.
Common errors are reading the head as aircraft position, forgetting the TO/FROM meaning, and treating bearing-pointer motion as a command instead of an orientation cue.

items.text: Going direct to a VOR is a setup-and-track procedure: tune the correct station, point at it, center a TO course, then keep the course centered with wind correction.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the desired VOR before trusting the display.
Select PFD source to VOR and select bearing pointer #1 to VOR.
Turn the shortest direction to place the head of bearing pointer #1 under the heading index.
Set a CDI course that centers the CDI with a TO indication; the PFD press-and-hold function can do this quickly.
Track the new course by flying a heading that keeps the CDI centered.
Do not skip station identification or fly to the wrong source just because a pointer is displayed.
A centered CDI is not the finish line; the next task is tracking, because wind will move the aircraft off the direct course unless you correct.

items.text: Tracking is not homing. Homing keeps turning toward the station; tracking corrects for wind so the ground track stays on the selected course.

children.text: Once established on course, hold heading equal to course until CDI or bearing-pointer movement shows drift.
Use tail-radial-wind: draw from the bearing-pointer tail toward the desired radial to visualize where the wind is coming from.
Use tail-radial-turn or the CDI bar to decide the turn back toward course; the aircraft symbol is where you are, and the deviation bar is where you need to go.
Use an intercept angle suited to distance and closure; other than extreme cases, 45 degrees should be the maximum needed.
After re-intercepting, crab into the wind to hold the course. If unsure, start with about 5 degrees and watch whether the CDI drifts the same way, reverses, or stays centered.
Near the station, CDI and bearing-pointer sensitivity increase because radial spacing tightens; keep corrections within about 10 degrees of wind-corrected heading to avoid chasing needles.
The event specifically values bearing-pointer-only orientation, so be ready to explain the same correction without a CDI.

items.text: Station passage is primarily recognized by the first positive TO-to-FROM change on the CDI as the aircraft passes directly over or abeam the radio facility.

children.text: Expect bearing-pointer and CDI sensitivity to increase close to a conventional NAVAID; do not treat every jump in the cone of confusion as a heading command.
Hold the planned wind-corrected heading through the unreliable portion instead of chasing rapid pointer movement.
After passage, let the bearing pointer stabilize before building the outbound intercept picture.

items.text: An over-the-station intercept is used to intercept and fly outbound on a specified radial immediately after station passage.

children.text: Use the six Ts one at a time: time as required, turn, time as required, transition, twist/intercept, and talk.

Turn the shortest direction to parallel or intercept the outbound course. For small course changes, parallel while the bearing pointer stabilizes; for course changes greater than 90 degrees, turn to an intercept heading.
Do not turn more than 45 degrees beyond the heading needed to parallel the new course.
Set the new outbound course in the CDI, confirm FROM, then use double-the-angle up to 45 degrees once the bearing pointer is stable.
Maintain the intercept heading until able to make a standard-rate turn onto the new course, then make required voice reports.
The goal is not to spin knobs perfectly while task-saturated; it is to keep the airplane controlled, start the correct outbound geometry, and establish the new course without delay.
Common errors are too much intercept, too little intercept, delaying the intercept setup, and trying to solve the whole six-T sequence at once.

items.text: Radial intercept procedures position the aircraft on a nearby radial or course without passing over the station.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the new course in the CDI: outbound uses the radial itself, while inbound uses the reciprocal.
Turn toward the CDI deviation bar so the head of the course arrow ends up in the top half of the HSI, and use tail-radial-turn to verify turn direction.
Use an intercept angle greater than the number of radials off course, but do not exceed 90 degrees.
A 45-degree intercept is normally sufficient for inbound and outbound intercepts.
If you are within about 10 radials and the CDI or bearing pointer is rapidly moving toward course, use double-the-angle instead of forcing the full 45-degree intercept.
For outbound double-the-angle, count from the bearing-pointer tail to the new course; for inbound, count from the bearing-pointer head to the new course.
Maintain the intercept heading until you can make a standard-rate turn onto the course, then track the radial or course with wind correction.
Close to the station, pointer movement accelerates; plan the intercept early enough that sensitivity does not make you chase.
Common errors are setting the reciprocal wrong, turning away from the needed intercept, using the wrong pointer end, and joining with too much or too little intercept.

studyNotes.summary: Build the HSI picture first, then use bearing-pointer and CDI movement to go direct, track, identify station passage, and intercept radials without chasing needles.

events.overview: I2202 builds the geometry that makes radio navigation usable when the clearance is not simply direct-to or radial tracking. Be ready to compute arc lead points, leave an arc on time, solve point-to-point headings, and handle oxygen-system or physiological problems without losing the instrument scan.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Arcing is flying at a constant DME from a NAVAID. You approximate the arc with small heading and bank changes; you are not trying to draw a perfect circle.

children.text: Proceed direct to the arc entry point defined by radial and DME.
Calculate the lead point, determine the turn direction, and begin a standard-rate turn at the lead point.
Continue the turn until the bearing-pointer head is on the 90-degree benchmark for the arc direction.
Check DME immediately after rollout and correct early instead of waiting for a large displacement.
In no wind, bearing-pointer head on the 90-degree benchmark means DME is constant.
Bearing-pointer head below the 90-degree benchmark means DME is increasing.
Bearing-pointer head above the 90-degree benchmark means DME is decreasing.
If inside the arc, maintain heading or place the bearing-pointer head up to 15 degrees below the benchmark; if outside, place it up to 15 degrees above the benchmark.
Common errors are late lead-point planning, turning the wrong direction, and overcorrecting DME instead of making small benchmark changes.

items.text: A radial-arc intercept transitions from tracking a radial to joining an arc at a specified DME.

children.text: For a standard-rate 90-degree turn, turn radius is 0.5% of groundspeed in NM; for example, 150 knots is about 0.75 NM.
If groundspeed is not available in time, KIAS may be used as a no-wind approximation.
When a full standard-rate turn is not appropriate, use 1.0% of groundspeed for a half-standard-rate lead point.
Apply the turn radius so the aircraft begins turning before the arc DME, then adjust for known wind.
Start the turn at the computed DME and roll toward the 90-degree bearing-pointer benchmark.
Check whether the first DME trend puts you inside or outside the arc, then correct with the arcing benchmark logic.
The briefing-guide emphasis is to know turn direction from the assigned arc direction before reaching the lead point.

items.text: An arc-radial intercept leaves an arc and joins an inbound or outbound radial. The key is calculating the lead radial early enough that the turn finishes on course.

children.text: Find radials per NM with the 60-to-1 rule: 60 divided by arc DME.
Find turn radius: 0.5% of groundspeed for standard-rate, or 1.0% for half-standard-rate.
Multiply turn radius by radials per NM; that product is the no-wind lead radial.
Set the CDI for the course you will intercept before reaching the lead radial, then begin the turn at the lead radial.
Greater arc DME means fewer lead radials because radials are farther apart.
Half-standard-rate turns need more lead radials than standard-rate turns because the turn takes longer.
Adjust the no-wind lead for known wind, then track the new radial or course after rollout.

items.text: An OBOGS malfunction is a crew-survival problem before it is a system-analysis problem. Keep flying, get a secure oxygen source, descend when required, and use the checklist.

children.text: An OBOGS FAIL warning can indicate low bleed-air pressure, low oxygen concentration, or an internal failure detected by the system.
OBOGS TEMP indicates a heat-exchanger failure and is treated as an OBOGS failure.
Physiological symptoms or zeolite-dust indications can occur without a warning light; coughing, respiratory irritation, or white dust in the mask still demand immediate action.
Engine failure, total electrical failure, main battery depletion, or battery failure removes OBOGS support.
Check both cockpits: supply ON, concentration MAX, pressure EMERGENCY, flow indication, hose/CRU-60/P connection, and mask seal.
If symptoms are recognized, immediately execute the OBOGS Failure/Overtemp/Physiological Symptoms procedure instead of troubleshooting first.
Emergency oxygen provides about 10 minutes; above 10,000 feet cockpit altitude, pulling the green ring is required before depletion risk becomes incapacitating.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL, secure OBOGS supply OFF as directed, and land as soon as practical.

items.text: Hypoxia and hyperventilation can feel similar early, so the safe cockpit answer is to protect oxygen first, then normalize breathing once the oxygen source is secure.

children.text: Hypoxia is oxygen deficiency in body tissues; early signs can include poor judgment, euphoria, fatigue, tunnel vision, dizziness, or headache.
Advanced hypoxia can progress to cyanosis, confusion, loss of coordination, unconsciousness, and incapacitation.
Susceptibility increases with factors such as fatigue, dehydration, illness, alcohol, medication, smoking, carbon monoxide exposure, temperature stress, and exertion.
Hyperventilation is abnormally rapid or deep breathing that lowers carbon dioxide.
Symptoms can include lightheadedness, tingling, drowsiness, muscle spasms, a feeling of suffocation, and in severe cases unconsciousness.
When breathing oxygen under increased pressure, breathe slightly slower and shallower than normal to avoid inducing hyperventilation.
If unsure which one you have, treat it like hypoxia first: secure oxygen, verify flow, descend as required, tell the other cockpit, then consciously slow and normalize breathing.
Do not let symptom analysis pull both pilots heads-down; keep one pilot flying and scanning.

items.text: Point-to-point navigation uses a VOR/DME or VORTAC to fly directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without waiting for radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID.
Set the desired radial in the CDI; this helps build the picture even when it is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the HSI compass card.
Plot the fix with the greater DME on the edge of the compass card and the smaller-DME fix proportionally closer to center.
Turn initially to a heading between the bearing-pointer head and the course-pointer head: split the heads.
Favor the bearing-pointer head when going to a smaller DME; favor the course-pointer head when going to a larger DME.
Use the pencil method to draw the present-position-to-desired-fix line, move that line to the center of the card, and read the updated no-wind heading.
Keep updating en route. If the line tilts right, turn right; if it tilts left, turn left.
As you near the fix, compare DME rate to radial-crossing rate.
If arriving at DME first, use the 90-degree benchmark to split the bearing pointer and desired radial; do not arc to the radial.
If arriving at the radial first, turn to track inbound or outbound as required toward the fix.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, splitting the wrong heads, using the reciprocal radial, failing to update the pencil solution, and trying to arc to the fix.

studyNotes.summary: Lead the arc, manage DME with bearing-pointer benchmarks, solve point-to-point geometry early, and treat oxygen or physiological symptoms as immediate crew-survival problems.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Holding entry begins before the fix: copy the clearance, determine the holding side and pattern direction, slow in time, and know the first outbound heading before crossing.

children.text: Start the speed reduction within 3 minutes or 5 NM of the holding fix when clearance beyond the fix has not been received.
The normal T-6B holding airspeed is 150 KIAS; published maximum holding speeds still matter for altitude and field-specific restrictions.
A standard pattern uses right turns; a non-standard pattern uses left turns. If turn direction is not stated, right turns are implied.
If timing is used, the inbound leg is normally 1 minute at or below 14,000 feet MSL and 1 1/2 minutes above 14,000 feet MSL.

For a standard pattern, parallel entry is used when the reciprocal of the holding course lies between the heading index and 110 degrees left; teardrop is between the heading index and 70 degrees right; otherwise use direct entry.
For a non-standard pattern, mirror the logic: parallel is to the right, teardrop is to the left, and direct is the remaining sector.
Standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees less than the reciprocal of the holding course; non-standard teardrop heading is 30 degrees more.
If the reciprocal is within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either entry is acceptable.
Use the six Ts to keep task order clean: time, turn, time, transition, twist, talk.
Report established in holding with position, time, and altitude when required; confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if needed.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial using tail-radial-turn and intercept the holding course promptly.

items.text: The no-wind orbit begins on the second passage of the holding fix and gives you the information needed to correct both heading and timing.

children.text: Cross the fix, reset elapsed time, and turn in the pattern direction to the no-wind outbound heading, which is the reciprocal of the holding course.
Start outbound timing when wings level or abeam the holding fix, whichever occurs last.
If abeam cannot be determined, start timing when wings level.
At the end of the outbound leg, turn inbound toward the holding radial and start inbound timing when wings level on course or with an appropriate intercept established.
An on-course inbound rollout suggests no crosswind component.
An undershoot suggests crosswind from the non-holding side.
An overshoot suggests crosswind from the holding side.
Once established inbound, use normal tracking procedures to find the wind-corrected heading and note the crab angle.
Note inbound time at the fix if timing corrections are required for the next orbit.
Keep basic airwork clean; altitude, heading, and airspeed errors contaminate the wind picture you are trying to measure.

items.text: Holding corrections apply the no-wind orbit lesson: correct outbound heading for drift, adjust outbound time for inbound timing, then refine on each orbit.

children.text: Triple the inbound drift correction for the outbound leg; for example, an 8-degree right crab inbound becomes a 24-degree left correction outbound.
Hold triple drift for no more than 1 minute outbound.
If the outbound leg continues beyond 1 minute, transition to single drift for the remaining time.
If no-wind inbound time exceeded 90 seconds, the first wind-corrected outbound time should be no less than 30 seconds.
Adjust outbound time to fix the previous inbound time. If inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound; if inbound was long, subtract time.
Subsequent orbits are fine-tuning passes, not proof that the first correction was bad.
Inbound legs are tracked on the holding course; outbound legs are flown as headings.
Keep fuel and EFC time in the scan, especially in stacked holding where vertical separation can be as little as 1000 feet.

Common errors are using the drift correction in the wrong direction, forgetting to transition from triple drift to single drift, trying to track outbound, and letting basic airwork or magnetic-variation confusion drive false corrections.

items.text: Battery and generator failure assumes the generator has failed and the main battery is depleted. In IMC, the problem is maintaining control with a stripped cockpit while getting below oxygen and pressurization risk.

children.text: Only auxiliary-battery-powered essentials remain: backup flight instrument, FIRE 1 detection, IRU, and VHF radio through the standby VHF control head.

Major losses include OBOGS, ICS, all electronic displays, PMU, starter, FIRE 2, landing-gear indicators, normal flap operation and indications, probes anti-ice, interior/exterior lighting, ECS/pressurization, UHF, GPS, VHF NAV, DME, transponder, and TCAS.
OBOGS is inoperative once the main battery is depleted or with battery failure, and the cockpit will depressurize when power to the battery bus is lost.
Initiate descent below 10,000 feet MSL as required.
Turn AUX BAT ON to power the backup flight instrument and standby VHF path for about 30 minutes.
Plan to extend the landing gear with the emergency extension system; emergency flaps will not be available if the main battery has failed, and flaps may retract if battery-bus power is lost.
Land as soon as possible.
In an instrument event, immediately transition your scan to the BFI, preserve attitude and airspeed, and use standby VHF/ATC help before task-saturating on lost displays.
A PAR or ASR/no-gyro recovery may be feasible if conditions, communication, and remaining instruments support it; brief it as a recovery option, not a guarantee.

studyNotes.summary: Enter holding deliberately, use the no-wind orbit to measure wind, correct with triple drift and timing, and keep the BFI/standby-VHF recovery plan ready for battery and generator failure.

The event standard is to copy and fly the clearance, transition cleanly from takeoff to instruments, stay ahead of en route setup, and execute procedure-turn, teardrop, arcing, and missed-approach procedures without losing the aircraft.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Clearance and departure procedures connect the IFR clearance, the departure method, and the instrument takeoff scan into one plan before the aircraft moves.

children.text: Copy the clearance deliberately: aircraft identification, clearance limit, departure type, route, altitude, departure frequency, transponder code, and any additional restrictions or holding instructions.
Before takeoff, review terrain, hazards, climb gradients, and the assigned departure type; set NAVAIDs and displays so the first navigation task is ready before brake release.
Keep the most likely emergency return approach available. Departure setup should answer where you will point the aircraft if the climb does not go normally.
Fly a normal takeoff, use outside references and the attitude indicator at liftoff, then transition fully to the instrument scan as visual cues diminish.
Set about 8 to 10 degrees nose high, trim, verify the climb on the altimeter and VSI, then raise the gear and flaps.
Maintain the initial attitude until about 180 KIAS unless the departure or aircraft performance requires a different climb profile.
For best-rate climb, use about 140 KIAS and 15 degrees nose high.
Lead level-offs with roughly 10 percent of the climb rate; for example, start adjusting about 200 feet early during a 2000 FPM climb.
If below climb speed, reduce power as the pitch comes down. If above climb speed, maintain power long enough to accelerate, then stabilize and trim.
Know the departure families: ODP, SID, radar departure, diverse departure, and VCOA.
For a diverse departure, climb to 400 feet AGL before turning and plan on at least 200 feet per NM, which is about 600 FPM at 180 KIAS.

items.text: En route procedures are the discipline that keeps the aircraft ahead of the next clearance, fix, approach setup, and descent requirement.

children.text: Use the assigned airway, radial, DME, or point-to-point clearance as the controlling navigation task; FMS shortcuts do not replace the radio-navigation procedure being trained.

For point-to-point navigation, tune and identify the NAVAID, set the desired radial, visualize the present and desired radial/DME positions, then split the bearing-pointer and course-pointer heads for the initial no-wind heading.
Update the point-to-point solution as DME and bearing change. If DME will arrive first, split the needle to slow DME change; if the radial arrives first, track inbound or outbound to the fix.
Use the ABCDs early enough to matter: ATIS, brief the approach and minimums, cockpit setup, and descent checklist before the IAF.
Plan NAVAID changeover at the published changeover point, halfway between facilities if no point is shown, or about 10 NM before an intersection when required.
Keep fuel, weather, recovery options, and approach request timing in the scan instead of waiting for the terminal area to force the workload.

items.text: A procedure turn reverses course inside protected airspace so the aircraft can intercept the final approach course from the proper side and altitude.

children.text: Do not fly a procedure turn when SNERT applies: straight-in clearance, NoPT routing, established in aligned holding and cleared for the approach, radar vectors to final, or a timed approach.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and prepare the six Ts.
At station passage, turn the shortest direction to parallel the outbound course. If that turn would exceed 90 degrees, use a 45-degree intercept.
Start 1 minute outbound when wings level or abeam, whichever occurs later; descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, normally adding power near 33 percent torque and re-trimming.
At 1 minute outbound, turn 45 degrees toward the protected side, start another 1-minute clock, and twist the inbound course.

At the end of the barb leg, turn 180 degrees opposite. If the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn with double-the-angle intercept; otherwise roll out on the barb heading for a 45-degree intercept.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and maintain altitude until slowing permits the descent.

items.text: A teardrop approach is another course-reversal option that uses an offset outbound leg toward the protected side before turning inbound.

children.text: A non-depicted teardrop may be used as a substitute for a depicted procedure turn when cleared for the approach; offset about 20 degrees from the final approach course toward the barb or protected side.
Remain within the published distance, typically 10 NM, and adjust the outbound leg for wind so the turn back inbound stays inside protected airspace.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS.
At station passage, turn toward the outbound teardrop course, start 2 minutes outbound when wings level or abeam, and descend if required with about 15 percent torque at 150 KIAS.
Level at the procedure-turn altitude, add power near 33 percent torque, and twist the inbound course at about 1.5 minutes outbound.
At 2 minutes outbound, turn in the depicted direction. Use double-the-angle if the bearing-pointer head is within 5 degrees of inbound; otherwise use a 45-degree intercept.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF and continue with the published approach.

items.text: Arcing approaches use DME to move around a facility until a lead radial or turn point places the aircraft on the final approach course.

children.text: Confirm DME is required by the approach title or equipment notes, such as VOR/DME or TACAN.
At the IAF, turn to place the bearing pointer on the 90-degree benchmark, comply with segment altitudes, and set the inbound course in the CDI.
Use radial-to-arc and arc-to-radial intercept techniques rather than chasing the needle after the turn point has passed.
For radial-to-arc intercepts, standard-rate lead DME is about 0.5 percent of groundspeed; half-standard-rate lead DME is about 1 percent of groundspeed.
For arc-to-radial intercepts, estimate radials per NM as 60 divided by arc DME, then multiply by turn radius to find the lead radial.
Published lead radials are normally based on 200 KTAS and half-standard-rate turns; at 150 KIAS, compute a standard-rate lead and adjust for wind.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and continue inbound on the published approach.

items.text: Missed approach procedures protect the climb after an approach can no longer be continued visually, safely, or within course guidance.

children.text: Execute the missed approach at the MAP or DA/DH when the runway environment is not in sight, required visibility is not available, or the aircraft is not in position for a normal landing.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, attempt to re-intercept, do not descend, and notify ATC.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs between the FAF and MAP, climb toward the missed-approach altitude and notify ATC. Obstacle protection is only assured along published or assigned segments.
In training, distinguish the published missed approach from an assigned climbout; fly the clearance you were given unless safety requires otherwise.
At the MAP, set PCL MAX, pitch 10 to 15 degrees nose high, verify two positive rates, then raise the gear.
Above 110 KIAS, raise the flaps, accelerate toward 180 KIAS, and adjust toward an 8 to 10 degree nose-high climb attitude.
Start a standard-rate turn as required to the missed-approach course or assigned heading, then report missed approach with the reason.
Once climbing and navigating, pass DRAFT as required: destination, route, altitude, fuel, and time en route.
Standard obstacle-clearance planning uses 200 feet per NM; the T-6B normally exceeds that at about 180 KIAS and roughly 2000 FPM, but higher published gradients still require performance planning.

studyNotes.summary: Copy and fly the IFR clearance, transition from takeoff to instruments, manage en route setup, and execute PT, teardrop, arcing, and missed-approach procedures with disciplined task flow.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: HILO approaches use a published holding pattern in lieu of a procedure turn to reverse direction and establish the aircraft inbound on the intermediate or final approach course.

children.text: The pattern is printed like holding, but it is treated like a course reversal. Only one turn in holding is authorized unless ATC clears additional turns.
A HILO approach always has a depicted FAF.
Case I permits descent to the holding altitude, then no lower until crossing the FAF.
Case II permits further descent once established inbound.
About 5 NM before the IAF, slow to 150 KIAS and prepare for a normal holding entry.

At the IAF, use the six Ts: no timing requirement at station passage, turn using the proper entry, start outbound timing when wings level or abeam, transition if descent is required, twist the inbound course, and talk as required.
If descending, use about 15 percent torque and 150 KIAS, then level at the required altitude before the next descent point.
Use tail-radial-turn and, if needed, double-the-angle intercept to establish inbound before crossing the holding fix.
Within 5 NM of the FAF, transition to before-approach configuration and continue with the published approach.

items.text: Holding is protected-airspace management: enter correctly, keep the inbound leg under control, and leave the pattern exactly as cleared.

children.text: Copy and read back the clearance, determine the holding side and turn direction, and slow to 150 KIAS within 3 minutes or 5 NM when required.
A standard pattern uses right turns; a non-standard pattern uses left turns.
Use the aircraft heading and the reciprocal of the holding course to choose direct, parallel, or teardrop entry.
If the reciprocal falls within 5 degrees of an entry boundary, either adjacent entry is acceptable.
Direct entry turns outbound in the pattern direction after fix passage.
Parallel entry flies outbound parallel to the inbound course, then turns opposite the pattern direction to intercept inbound.
Teardrop entry turns 30 degrees toward the holding side from the reciprocal of the holding course.
Use the six Ts at the fix and on each turn so timing, turns, configuration, CDI setting, and required reports stay in order.
Use tail-radial-turn to decide the inbound turn direction when tracking back toward the holding radial.
Triple the inbound drift correction on the outbound leg for up to 1 minute, then transition to single drift if the outbound leg continues.
Adjust outbound time by the inbound timing error: if inbound was 10 seconds short, add 10 seconds outbound; if it was long, subtract time.
Report position, time, and altitude when required, and confirm EFC at least 5 minutes prior if needed.

items.text: A shuttle descent is an ATC-directed descent inside holding that preserves the stack while moving the aircraft to a lower altitude.

children.text: Report leaving the current altitude for the assigned altitude.
Set about 15 percent torque, lower the nose to maintain 150 KIAS, and re-trim without letting the holding pattern unravel.
Lead the level-off by about 50 feet, add power near 33 percent torque, raise the nose to level flight, and re-trim.
The common trap is fixation: watching altitude so hard that the pattern drifts, or watching the pattern so hard that the level-off is missed.

items.text: Intersections are fixes that drive airway changes, timing reports, holding entries, approach transitions, missed approaches, and configuration or altitude tasks.

children.text: Use the primary NAVAID for the course being flown and the secondary NAVAID only as the crosscut used to identify the fix.
For VOR/DME intersections, track the primary course to the fix DME, note the time if required, then either continue outbound or start the standard-rate turn to the new course.
When turning to a new course, set up the next course within about 10 NM, maintain the wind-corrected heading until the turn lead, then intercept promptly if early or late.
For VOR-only intersections, estimate the fix time, tune the secondary NAVAID about 3 minutes prior, and watch the crosscut bearing-pointer tail.
If the tail is still more than 10 radials from the fix, retune the primary, wait briefly, and recheck.
When within 10 radials, hold heading until the tail rises to the crossing radial, then note time and continue or turn as cleared.
Late secondary setup, wrong turn lead, and trying to force the aircraft exactly over the fix when that is not required are the common errors.
For GPS fly-over waypoints, confirm the waypoint is next in sequence, cross it, then update course after the active leg changes.
For GPS fly-by waypoints, the system anticipates the turn; start the standard-rate turn when the CDI flashes and re-intercept promptly if the timing is off.

items.text: Oil system malfunctions are PEL-driving problems unless the indication is clearly limited to a brief amber caution with normal oil pressure.

children.text: Use this procedure for a red OIL PX warning, amber OIL PX caution, oil-pressure fluctuations, oil temperature out of limits, or visible oil leak.
If only the amber OIL PX caution illuminates, terminate maneuvering and check oil pressure. If oil pressure is normal, continued operation may be appropriate.
A momentary amber OIL PX during maneuvering may not indicate a malfunction, and simultaneous red and amber OIL PX with normal oil pressure indicates an SCU failure.
If an OIL PX warning occurs with oil pressure below 5 psi, the OIL TRX circuit breaker may be checked and reset if open, but troubleshooting must not delay aircraft control or the landing decision.

For red OIL PX, amber OIL PX lasting more than 5 seconds, oil-pressure fluctuations, or oil temperature out of limits, set PCL to the minimum necessary to intercept the ELP and avoid unnecessary PCL movement.
Execute a PEL. Higher power may aggravate the condition, so use only what the profile requires.
Normal steady-state oil pressure is 90 to 120 psi; oil pressure less than 90 psi at flight idle or above is indicative of a malfunction.
Normal flight oil temperature is 10 to 105 degrees C, with 106 to 110 degrees C limited to 10 minutes.

studyNotes.summary: Fly the HILO as protected course-reversal holding, keep holding corrections and shuttle descents organized, identify intersections on time, and treat oil-system indications as PEL decision points.

The standard is to follow controller instructions promptly without surrendering aircraft control, orientation, minimums discipline, or the propeller-malfunction branch logic.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: PAR is a precision radar approach in which the final controller gives azimuth and glideslope corrections to guide the aircraft to DA/DH.

children.text: Expect surveillance radar vectors toward final, normally with standard-rate turns not exceeding 30 degrees AOB and prompt compliance with assigned headings and altitudes.
Complete landing checks, review minimums, lost-communication instructions, missed-approach or climbout instructions, and keep position orientation with available NAVAIDs.
PAR equipment provides precise runway centerline guidance, elevation guidance, and range; typical training limits are about 10 NM range, 20 degrees azimuth, and 7 degrees elevation.
When transferred to final controller, include gear status if required and be in before-approach configuration before glideslope intercept.
Begin descent only when told "on glideslope," not when told "approaching glidepath."
At glideslope intercept, use about 24 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and roughly 600 FPM. Pitch controls airspeed and power controls glideslope, with small prompt corrections.
At DA/DH, continue only if the runway environment is in sight and the landing is safe; do not level at DA/DH.

If communication is lost for more than 1 minute on vectors to final, more than 15 seconds on ASR or PAR without glideslope final, or more than 5 seconds on PAR final with glideslope, attempt secondary or tower frequency.
Proceed VFR if able, or execute the approved non-radar approach or published radar lost-communication procedure.
Miss immediately if directed by controller, tower, RDO, or wheels watch; if unsafe; or at DA/DH without required visual references.

items.text: PAR W/O GS is a nonprecision radar approach: the final controller gives precise azimuth and range, but no glideslope.

children.text: The approach may start with surveillance radar vectors and then transfer to PAR final for azimuth-only final guidance.
Because no glideslope is provided, the controller states the MAP location and mile markers and may direct descent to MDA or step-down fixes.
The more precise PAR azimuth and range may support a lower MDA than an ASR approach, but it remains a nonprecision approach.
Use about 200 KIAS on downwind and 150 KIAS on base; if extended on final or dogleg, maintain 200 KIAS until within about 15 NM.
Transition to before-approach configuration and complete landing checks on final or dogleg no later than 15 NM.
With recommended altitudes, use about 24 percent torque and 120 KIAS, adjusting descent to meet the altitude gates.
Without recommended altitudes, use about 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM to MDA.
Lead the level-off about 100 feet before MDA, maintain MDA and assigned heading to the MAP, then land only if visual and safe.

items.text: ASR is a nonprecision radar approach using airport surveillance radar for course guidance throughout the approach.

children.text: Expect heading corrections, range calls, the MAP location, and descent instructions to MDA or step-down fixes.
Because the controller is not providing glideslope, you are responsible for a stable descent profile, MDA level-off, and timing the decision at the MAP.
If circling is planned, provide the aircraft approach category when needed so the correct circling MDA is used.
Acknowledge controller instructions unless told not to acknowledge; slow or missed readbacks are a major radar-approach error.
Do not descend to MDA early just to get level. Heavy precipitation and low altitude can increase ground clutter and degrade radar contact.
If radar contact is lost and the runway environment is not in sight, execute the missed approach or assigned climbout.
At the MAP, guidance terminates; if the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe, go missed.

items.text: Recommended altitudes are pilot-requested altitude gates on final that help stabilize a nonprecision radar approach to MDA.

children.text: They are based on the procedure descent gradient and are normally issued at each mile on final down to the last mile at or above MDA.
Use them as a rate-control aid, not permission to descend below published step-down restrictions or below MDA.
With recommended altitudes, adjust descent rate to meet each gate while keeping 120 KIAS and a stable configuration.
Without recommended altitudes, manage your own descent rate, level 100 feet prior to MDA, and maintain MDA until the MAP.

items.text: IMC emergency discussion starts with aircraft control, terrain clearance, ATC coordination, and crew coordination before checklist detail.

children.text: NATOPS procedures are the best available procedures, but they do not replace judgment when weather, terrain, multiple emergencies, or aircraft state change the problem.
Use the basic order: maintain aircraft control, analyze the situation, take proper action, and land as soon as conditions permit.
Inadvertent IMC, spatial disorientation, malfunction, or IMC abort requires a stable instrument scan before troubleshooting expands.

Maintain aircraft control, transition fully to instruments, and climb immediately toward the applicable ERAA or local safe-altitude guidance as conditions permit; squawk as required and tell ATC your intentions.
On an IFR clearance, coordinate deviations with ATC unless the emergency requires immediate action.
A declared emergency and radar vectors to a suitable recovery field may be the safest option; brief what you need from ATC before task saturation takes over.
The pilot at the controls executes critical action memory items and PIC-directed actions while preserving the scan.

items.text: Propeller malfunctions include uncommanded power change, failure to produce expected power, and uncommanded propeller feathering; the branch point is whether enough usable power remains for a PEL.

children.text: Engine rollback may show decreasing power or thrust, decreasing fuel flow and N1 with PMU on, or a step change in power with PMU off.
Uncommanded propeller feathering may show rapid NP decrease, torque increase, increased propeller noise, thrust loss, vibration, and degraded glide performance.
Prop-sleeve touchdown may cause NP fluctuations, torque increase, thrust decrease, vibration, and possible CHIP indication.
Set PCL to mid range, physically halfway between IDLE and MAX, then set the PMU switch OFF.
If NP is stable below 40 percent, pull the PROP SYS circuit breaker. Stable means below 40 percent with no upward change for 3 seconds at constant airspeed and torque.
Expect the propeller to unfeather in roughly 15 to 20 seconds if the procedure is effective.
Use PCL as required after the initial actions, monitoring torque, ITT, NP, and rate of descent.
If sufficient power is available, execute a PEL.

If power is insufficient, consider leaving the engine operating at mid-range PCL only when uncommanded feather is suspected and engine limits remain acceptable; otherwise transition toward engine shutdown, forced landing, or ejection as directed by the checklist and aircraft state.

With the PROP SYS circuit breaker pulled and PMU OFF, the feather dump solenoid is unpowered; the propeller feathers more slowly as oil pressure decreases, and glide performance may be considerably reduced.

If VSI remains greater than 1500 FPM at 125 KIAS with gear, flaps, and speed brake retracted and only 4 to 6 percent torque, increase torque as needed up to limits. If unable to reduce descent rate, set PCL OFF.

studyNotes.summary: Fly radar approaches through controller instructions without losing minimums discipline, IMC emergency priorities, or the propeller-malfunction decision tree.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: Night cockpit setup is about preserving the scan, protecting night adaptation, and making every needed chart, light, and control usable before workload rises.

children.text: Set interior lighting early enough to read instruments and charts without washing out dark adaptation or making the display picture harder to interpret.
Know where utility, map, and kneeboard lighting are before the approach sequence; do not discover the lighting plan during a frequency change or missed approach.
Dim bright displays gradually and keep the standby instruments and backup lighting in the scan.
At night, a cockpit lighting, display, radio, or electrical problem can become a recovery-timing problem faster than it would in daylight.
Use exterior lighting with airfield courtesy and local procedures, especially around ground crews, other aircraft, and low-visibility taxi conditions.
If field orientation becomes uncertain, stop or stabilize the aircraft and re-sort the picture instead of continuing while unsure.

items.text: A SID is a published IFR departure procedure that provides obstacle clearance and transitions the aircraft from the terminal area toward the en route structure.

children.text: Before takeoff, review the entire SID, terrain, hazards, climb gradient, crossing restrictions, transition, and lost-communication or emergency-return implications.
Set NAVAIDs, displays, and courses required for the first turns and altitude restrictions. If FMS use is authorized, confirm the loaded procedure matches the clearance.
Keep the primary recovery approach available in case the departure must become an emergency return.
Fly the cleared procedure, not just the chart title. Understand whether the clearance includes climb-via language, radar vectors, or a named transition.
If the SID requires a climb gradient above standard, confirm aircraft performance before accepting the plan.
Common errors are briefing only the first heading, missing an altitude or crossing restriction, and launching with the wrong NAVAID or display source selected.

items.text: RVFAC uses radar vectors to place the aircraft on the final approach course, which can reduce terminal workload only if orientation and setup stay ahead.

children.text: Approach control vectors using minimum vectoring altitude charts, but the pilot still keeps terrain and procedure SA.
Crosscheck assigned altitudes against the approach, NAVAIDs, and chart picture; query ATC if the vector or altitude does not make sense.
Maintain the last assigned heading and altitude until established on the approach or cleared otherwise.
Use 200 KIAS on downwind, 150 KIAS on base, and 200 KIAS on extended final or dogleg until within about 15 NM unless directed otherwise.
Tune and identify the appropriate NAVAID, verify PFD source/configuration, and set the final approach course in the CDI.
If a FAF is depicted, transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF when heading is within 90 degrees of the final approach course.
If no FAF is depicted, transition once established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach.

items.text: ILS/LOC approaches use localizer guidance for precise lateral control; ILS adds glideslope for a precision approach, while LOC-only is nonprecision.

children.text: The localizer is much more sensitive than VOR guidance, about 1.25 degrees per dot, so course corrections must be small and prompt.
Set the published front course to avoid reverse-sensing errors and confirm the PFD source changes to LOC.
If the localizer is inoperative, the ILS is not authorized. If the glideslope is unavailable, fly the LOC procedure using nonprecision rules and minimums.
For a single-piloted T-6B, do not plan below the applicable absolute single-pilot minimums even if the charted ILS minimums are lower.
Use D LIDS: DME hold if required, localizer tune/identify/monitor, inbound course set, display source to LOC, and speed appropriate to the transition.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAF with an intercept angle at or below 90 degrees, or when the glideslope comes alive if that occurs first.
At glideslope intercept, use about 24 percent torque, descend on course and glideslope to DA/DH, and remember that pitch primarily controls airspeed while power controls glideslope.
At DA/DH, decide: land if the runway environment is in sight and landing is safe; otherwise execute the missed approach. Do not level at DA/DH.
For LOC-only, start backup timing at the nonprecision FAF if timing is available, then descend with about 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM.
Lead the MDA level-off by about 100 feet, use about 42 percent torque to stabilize, and maintain MDA until the MAP.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs before the FAF, re-intercept and do not descend below the FAF altitude until on scale.
If full-scale CDI deflection occurs inside the FAF, turn to reestablish, climb to the appropriate MAP altitude while respecting restrictions, and execute the missed approach at the MAP.
If more than 1 dot below glideslope before the MAP, do not descend below LOC MDA until reestablished; if more than 2 dots above glideslope, continue as LOC-only.

items.text: PTP is a VOR/DME or VORTAC technique for navigating directly from present position to a radial/DME fix without radar vectors.

children.text: Tune, identify, and monitor the NAVAID, then set the desired radial in the CDI even if that is not the heading you will fly.
Visualize the station at the center of the compass card. Put the larger DME on the outer edge at its radial and the smaller DME proportionally closer to the center.
Split the bearing-pointer and course-pointer heads for the initial heading, favoring the bearing pointer when going to smaller DME and the course pointer when going to larger DME.
Use the pencil method or compass-card picture to update heading as the line to the fix changes.
If DME will arrive first, use the 90-degree benchmark to slow DME change; do not turn the maneuver into an arc.
If the radial arrives first, track inbound or outbound on the radial to the fix.
A bearing-pointer head above the 90-degree benchmark means DME is decreasing; below the benchmark means DME is increasing.
Common errors are delaying the initial turn, plotting the reciprocal radial, failing to update heading, or tracking the radial too early.

items.text: Any emergency procedure in this event should be briefed as a decision process: maintain control, execute memory items when required, back up with the checklist, coordinate with ATC, and choose the correct recovery branch.

children.text: For fuel-system emphasis, low fuel pressure and high fuel flow both point toward a PEL rather than extended troubleshooting.
For low fuel pressure, execute the PEL and place the boost pump ON. If the FUEL PX warning remains illuminated, the high-pressure fuel pump is suction feeding and engine operation is time-limited.
Unless a greater emergency exists, do not reset an open BOOST PUMP circuit breaker.
For high fuel flow, execute a PEL. Reducing power when ITT remains within limits may risk flameout, while high power with high ITT may aggravate the malfunction.
At night or in IMC, declare early when needed and tell ATC what recovery you need before radio, lighting, or display workload steals the scan.
A strong EP brief explains the cue, the immediate action, the N/W/C that changes the answer, and the follow-on branch: continue, PEL, force-land, or eject.

studyNotes.summary: Set the night cockpit before workload rises, then fly SID, RVFAC, ILS/LOC, and PTP tasks while keeping emergency-procedure branch logic close at hand.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: GPS procedures begin with database and display discipline: the FMS can reduce workload only when the active waypoint, CDI source, and bearing-pointer picture are correct.

children.text: For direct-to navigation, load the desired waypoint, make it active, select FMS as the PFD source, and use the FMS bearing pointer to orient before tracking the CDI.
For GPS intersections, confirm the next waypoint is loaded on the LEGS page before the aircraft reaches the fix.
Approaching a waypoint, the NAV page cue changes from magenta to white over a magenta background, and along-track distance counts down toward 0.0 when crossing directly over the waypoint.
A fly-over waypoint is annotated with /O and must be crossed before turning; after passage, the pointer sequences to the next waypoint.
A fly-by waypoint gives turn anticipation. When the CDI deviation bar flashes, begin a standard-rate turn and intercept or roll out on the new course.
For timing or reporting at a fly-by waypoint, note the time when wings are level and the aircraft is on course or established on an intercept.

items.text: GPS allowable operations are limited by the published procedure, current database, approach title, and whether the underlying NAVAID must still be monitored.

children.text: A published IAP, DP, or STAR must be retrieved by name from a current navigation database; do not manually build an IFR procedure waypoint by waypoint.
Suitable RNAV/GPS may be used to determine position or distance from VOR, VOR/DME, VORTAC, TACAN, NDB, compass locator, DME fixes, and named fixes.
GPS may be used to navigate to or from VOR, TACAN, NDB, compass locator, or DME fixes, and may be used for holding or DME arcs when the rules allow.
Do not use GPS as lateral guidance on a localizer-based final segment unless GPS is in the approach title or the procedure is otherwise specifically authorized.
GPS cannot substitute for the NAVAID providing final approach course guidance, except for procedures titled with GPS or "or GPS" authorization.
If flying the final segment of a VOR, TACAN, or NDB approach with GPS substitution, the underlying NAVAID must be operational and monitored for course alignment.
An alternate airport used for planning must have at least one available non-GPS approach; do not build the alternate plan solely on GPS substitution.
The published chart takes precedence over the GPS display when magnetic variation or database presentation creates a disagreement.

items.text: GPS approaches require correct loading, TAA altitude discipline, approach-mode verification, and a deliberate missed-approach sequence.

children.text: Use LDDHA: load the approach with the correct transition, direct to the IAWP or build the vector-to-final leg as cleared, display FMS, verify any hold or HILO, and confirm APR mode.
A Terminal Arrival Area transitions aircraft from the RNAV en route structure to the terminal area while providing obstacle clearance.
Being cleared direct to an IAF or IF/IAF without an approach clearance does not authorize descent to the lower TAA altitude.
Once cleared for the approach, descend only as authorized by the depicted TAA sector, feeder route, ATC clearance, and published restrictions.
Slow to 150 KIAS within 5 NM of the IAWP when not on radar vectors, then transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP.
Expect HSI scale-change advisory about 3 NM before the FAWP and verify APR annunciation about 2 NM before the FAWP.
At the FAWP, use the six Ts and descend with about 15 to 20 percent torque, 120 KIAS, and no more than 1000 FPM to LNAV MDA.
The T-6B is certified for RNAV (GPS) approaches to LNAV MDA minimums; do not use VNAV, LNAV/VNAV, or LPV-style vertical minimums.
Level at MDA and continue to the MAWP. If the runway environment is not in sight or landing is unsafe at the MAWP, execute the missed approach.
The FMS will not automatically sequence the missed approach at the MAWP; select MISS APR and execute when the missed approach is required.
If APR mode is not active by 2 NM from the FAWP or GPS integrity is lost before the FAWP, use a backup approach if authorized; otherwise continue at FAWP altitude to the MAWP and go missed.
If GPS integrity is lost inside the FAWP, transition to a backup if authorized, climb to missed-approach altitude, track to the MAWP, execute the missed, and tell ATC as soon as practical.

items.text: GPS holding uses the same holding logic as radio holding, but waypoint passage and abeam cues come from FMS sequencing and along-track distance.

children.text: Confirm the holding waypoint, inbound course, turn direction, leg length or timing, altitude, and EFC before the fix.
When holding at a GPS waypoint, abeam occurs when along-track distance reaches its minimum and begins increasing.
If abeam cannot be determined, start outbound timing when wings are level after the outbound turn.
Use normal holding corrections: track inbound, apply outbound wind correction, and keep speed, altitude, EFC, and fuel in the scan.

items.text: GPS flight modes change CDI sensitivity and required navigation performance, so mode awareness is part of the instrument scan.

children.text: ENR mode uses 2 NM full-scale deflection, or 1 NM per dot.
TERM mode uses 1 NM full-scale deflection, or 0.5 NM per dot.
APR mode uses 0.3 NM full-scale deflection, or 0.15 NM per dot, and displays APR plus the green NPA annunciator.
Departure starts in TERM and normally changes to ENR either more than 33 NM from the origin or above 16,000 feet AGL from origin elevation.
ENR changes to TERM when within 30 NM of the destination and below 15,000 feet AGL from destination elevation.
TERM changes to APR about 2 NM before the FAWP when a valid GPS approach is loaded and integrity is available at the current position, FAWP, and MAP.
APR returns to TERM once MISS APR is selected, with HSI scale returning to 1 NM full scale and RNP returning to 1.0 NM.
At the MAP, the bearing pointer flips and distance-to-go increases, but guidance remains along extended final until MISS APR is manually initiated.

studyNotes.summary: Use the FMS deliberately: load only current database procedures, verify GPS authorization, manage TAA and APR-mode cues, and manually command missed-approach sequencing when required.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A STAR is an ATC-coded IFR arrival route that simplifies clearance delivery and transitions the aircraft from en route structure toward an instrument approach.

children.text: You must have the STAR chart available to accept the clearance.
RNAV STARs require an FMS-equipped aircraft and a current database procedure.
Mandatory crossing altitudes and speeds are binding when included in the clearance; "expect" altitudes and speeds are planning information until ATC assigns them.
MEAs are not STAR restrictions, but you must still remain above required en route minimum altitudes.
"Cleared the arrival" normally means fly the published lateral route and published speeds while maintaining the last assigned altitude until ATC authorizes descent.
"Descend via" authorizes lateral and vertical navigation on the arrival to comply with published altitude and speed restrictions, but not below the published bottom altitude.
When checking in on a new frequency while descending via, include the phrase "descending via" so the next controller knows your vertical clearance.
Do not use "expect" altitudes or speeds for lost-communication planning unless ATC specifically issued them as part of a further clearance.

items.text: The Trouble T symbol tells you non-standard takeoff minimums, obstacle information, or special departure procedures may apply.

children.text: The symbol appears on IAP, DP, ODP, or SID charts and points you to the takeoff minimums and obstacle-departure information for that airport.
The details are grouped by airport in the front section of the approach-plate or TPP booklet, usually alphabetically.
Trouble T is an obstacle-clearance alert; Navy takeoff weather minimums are related planning data but come from CNAF/OPNAV rules.
Read the actual text before departure. The symbol alone does not tell you the climb gradient, runway-specific restriction, or required route.
Some departures may still be legal with standard minimums if the aircraft meets a specific climb or routing requirement.
Convert any climb gradient in feet per NM into a required climb rate using groundspeed in NM per minute times the required feet per NM.

items.text: Obstacle Departure Procedures provide obstacle clearance from the terminal area to the en route structure when obstacles require something more specific than a diverse departure.

children.text: ODPs are labeled with "OBSTACLE" in the title on DoD/FAA charts.
They are developed when obstacles penetrate the departure obstacle-clearance surface and may be textual, graphical, or RNAV.
There is normally one ODP per runway, designed to provide the least restrictive obstacle-clearance route.
ODPs are not usually assigned by ATC unless needed for separation; the pilot must determine whether one exists and whether it should be flown.
Plan for higher-than-standard climb gradients, initial headings away from the intended course, special altitude restrictions, and close-in obstacles.
Check whether aircraft performance can meet the required gradient under expected conditions, including any emergency or degraded-performance plan.
If using an ODP, file or tell ATC clearly enough that the first controller understands the intended departure path.

items.text: Obtaining an IFR clearance from an uncontrolled airport is a preflight planning item, not a radio scramble at the hold-short line.

children.text: Common options include telephone clearance through FSS or ATC, published radio frequencies, RCO, UNICOM relay, direct ATC phone number, GCO, or a VFR departure to pick up IFR in the air when weather and rules allow.
A GCO is a remote ground-to-ground link used from the ground; four microphone clicks normally connects to ATC and six to AFSS when configured that way.
Plan the method before startup and have the backup method ready if the first contact path is saturated or unavailable.
If ATC issues a clearance void time, be airborne before the void time or contact ATC with intentions.
ATC also issues a notification time, no more than 30 minutes after the void time; failure to contact by that time can trigger overdue-aircraft action.
Once the void time passes, the IFR slot is released. Do not depart IFR on an expired clearance.
If departing VFR to pick up IFR, maintain VFR until the IFR clearance is received and accepted.

sections.title: Obtaining IFR Clearance from Uncontrolled Airports

items.text: RVFAC for RNAV approaches uses radar vectors to establish the aircraft on an RNAV final approach course while the FMS is configured for the correct leg and approach mode.

children.text: Load the RNAV approach from the current database with the correct runway and transition or vectors-to-final setup.
For a vector to final, build the final approach waypoint as the active leg, extend the intercept as required by the FMS, execute the modification, and set the PFD source to FMS.
Maintain ATC-assigned heading and altitude until established on the final approach course and cleared for the approach or otherwise cleared lower.
Keep the chart ahead of the FMS: the published procedure, not the magenta line alone, controls altitude, course, and missed-approach requirements.
Use RVFAC speed discipline from the radio-instrument pattern: 200 KIAS on downwind or extended final outside about 15 NM, and 150 KIAS on base unless directed otherwise.
Transition to before-approach configuration within 5 NM of the FAWP when established or being established on final.
Verify the HSI scale-change cue near 3 NM from the FAWP and APR annunciation near 2 NM from the FAWP.
If APR does not arm or GPS integrity is not available, use the authorized backup plan or continue at the appropriate altitude to the missed-approach point and execute the missed.

items.text: Obtaining IFR Clearance from Uncontrolled Airports

studyNotes.summary: Read arrivals and departures as clearances with consequences: know what ATC has authorized, what the chart requires, and how the FMS/RNAV setup supports the procedure.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A no-gyro approach is available under radar control when the directional gyro or stabilized compass information is inoperative or unreliable.

children.text: Tell ATC the heading system is unreliable and request a no-gyro PAR, ASR, PAR without glideslope, or no-gyro vectors to a visual approach if conditions support it.
Comply with normal PAR or ASR configuration, minimums, lost-communication, and missed-approach procedures; no-gyro only changes how turns are commanded.
ATC may also initiate no-gyro vectors if they observe incorrect directional responses.
Before final, make all turns at standard rate unless the controller directs otherwise, and start the turn immediately when told "turn left" or "turn right."
Stop the turn immediately when told "stop turn."
On final, use half-standard-rate turns unless the controller directs another rate.
Acknowledge instructions unless ATC states no further acknowledgements are required.

The common errors are slow turn compliance, using the wrong turn rate, arriving on final late to before-approach configuration, and confusing missed-approach, climbout, and lost-communication instructions.

items.text: A BFI approach is the control plan when the PFD or primary attitude/air-data picture is unusable because of ADC, IRU, IAC, or display failures.

children.text: Transition to the BFI first, then stabilize straight-and-level flight before troubleshooting expands.
Use coordinated rudder and aileron to level the wings, set a known pitch attitude, and crosscheck airspeed, altitude, vertical speed, and performance.
Complete the applicable NATOPS emergency procedure only after the aircraft is under control.
The BFI does not present turn information like the PFD; use attitude, heading trend, and the 10 percent or 20 percent bank-start rules for half-standard-rate or standard-rate turns.
The sideslip indicator is on top of the roll pointer and moves with it, which looks different from the PFD.
The altimeter uses 20-foot increments, the heading display shows only a partial scale, and VSI is a digital readout with up or down trend.
Use small corrections. The BFI workload trap is overcontrolling because the display looks unfamiliar.
A BFI recovery may pair naturally with no-gyro vectors or a radar approach because ATC can reduce heading-reference workload while the pilot preserves attitude and performance.
If communications, transponder, or remaining avionics are degraded too, declare the emergency and ask for the simplest recovery that preserves terrain clearance and workload margin.

studyNotes.summary: Let radar control reduce the heading workload, transition to the BFI before troubleshooting, and fly the degraded-instrument approach with small corrections and clear missed-approach logic.

studyNotes.headline: Discussion Items

items.text: A high-altitude approach transitions the aircraft from high-altitude structure to the final approach course by combining a penetration descent with an instrument approach.

children.text: Complete the Descent Checklist before terminal entry and review the chart for printed penetration instructions, altitude restrictions, DME restrictions, and the final approach transition.

At the IAF, execute the 6 Ts. Time only when required, turn as published or in the shortest direction to parallel the penetration course, transition into the descent, twist the appropriate course, and talk when a report is required.
Use the published high-altitude chart, not memory of a local example, to decide whether the penetration is teardrop, arcing, or straight-in.
Fly 200-250 KIAS during the penetration and set power and speed brake as required for about 2000-4000 FPM until approaching the level-off.
About 1000 feet before level-off, reduce the descent rate to 500-1500 FPM so the aircraft does not arrive low, fast, or task-saturated.
Level segments of the penetration may be flown at normal cruise, then transition to low-altitude approach procedures once established inbound and configured to before-approach condition.
T-6B high-altitude charts use Category C minimums; do not look for Category B minimums on those charts.
For a teardrop penetration, begin the penetration turn at one-half the initial altitude or the published penetration turn, as applicable, and use 30 degrees AOB.
During the last half of the teardrop turn, if the bearing pointer is not within 5 degrees of the inbound course, stop the turn with a 45-degree intercept.
If the bearing pointer is within 5 degrees of the inbound course, continue the turn and roll out with a double-the-angle intercept.
For an arcing penetration, use about 1 percent of groundspeed for lead computations when intercepting an arc or a radial from an arc, and do not exceed 30 degrees AOB.

items.text: Non-radar communications replace radar monitoring with pilot position, altitude, and time reports that let ATC maintain IFR separation.

children.text: In both radar and non-radar environments, report vacating an assigned altitude, VFR-on-top altitude changes, inability to climb or descend at least 500 FPM, missed approach, and a true-airspeed change of 5 percent or 10 knots from the filed value.

Also report reaching or leaving a holding fix unless the military training/radar exception applies, any loss of IFR navigation or communications capability, safety-of-flight information, and unforecast or hazardous weather.
When reporting equipment loss, include the aircraft identification, equipment affected, and the effect on IFR capability.
In a non-radar environment, also report leaving the FAF inbound on a non-precision approach or leaving the outer marker or substitute fix inbound on a precision approach.
Send a corrected estimate any time a previously submitted ETA is more than 3 minutes in error.
On initial non-radar contact, include present position, altitude, and the estimate for the next reporting point; in radar service, altitude and terminal information are normally the focus.
Report over compulsory reporting points shown by solid triangles, and over every point used to define direct-route legs when operating non-radar.
Use a courtesy call before a long report, then give the PTAPTP sequence: current position, time, altitude; next position and ETA; next succeeding position.
When ATC advises radar contact, discontinue normal position reports; resume them if radar contact is lost or radar service is terminated.
